The evening air of the royal gardens carried the soft, honeyed scent of Olympian jasmine—a flower Godric had personally resurrected from the genetic memory of his fallen kingdom and cultivated across ten thousand palace terraces. Kaedan sat on a weathered stone bench, his hands clasped tightly in his lap, watching his uncle tend to the flowering vines with the patient, careful movements of a man who had spent ten thousand years learning the delicate art of gentle hands. The sun was setting over the capital, painting the sky in shades of burnt orange and royal purple, and the distant sounds of the city—laughter, music, the quiet hum of a civilization at peace—drifted up from the valleys below like the contented sigh of a sleeping child.

Godric looked exactly as he always did. Forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, his heavily muscled frame draped in simple, dark garments that did nothing to conceal the sheer physical density of his form. His short salt-and-pepper hair caught the fading light, and his neatly trimmed beard framed a face that was, at this moment, creased with an expression of absolute, peaceful contentment. He was humming softly—the lullaby, Kaedan recognized now, the one he had sung to his daughters ten thousand years ago in the gardens of a kingdom that no longer existed.

The question had been forming in Kaedan's mind for months. It had crystallized during the reading of the journals, had sharpened during the long, sleepless nights that followed, had pressed against his teeth like a physical weight demanding release. He was twenty-two years old. He had read the accumulated terror of a million years of court wizards. He had learned that his beloved uncle was not merely powerful—he was an absolute, an impossibility, a being whose slightest expression of power could annihilate the omniverse an infinite number of times without effort.

And yet, sitting here in the garden, watching Godric gently prune a wilting leaf from the jasmine vine with the tender precision of a master gardener, Kaedan could not reconcile the journals with the man. The journals spoke of an apex god predator, a merciless, cruel, unforgiving tyrant who reduced civilizations to screaming, eternal agony without a second thought. But the man in front of him was Uncle Godric—the man who had taught him to read, who had attended his birthday celebrations, who had personally brewed medicinal tea for him when he was sick, who had always, always been there, a warm, steady, comforting presence in his life.

"Uncle Godric," Kaedan said, his voice barely above a whisper.

Godric looked up from the jasmine, his hands stilling on the vine. "Yes, my boy?"

"Does it ever become lonely?"

The question hung in the air between them, fragile and trembling like a soap bubble drifting through a storm. Kaedan felt his heart hammering against his ribs, felt the cold sweat breaking out across his palms, felt the weight of his own audacity pressing down on his shoulders like a physical force. He had just asked the most powerful being in existence—the entity who could erase him with less than a thought, who had retroactively deleted the concept of logical opposition from the omniverse, who had activated an eternal recursive loop of self-improvement that would never end—if he was lonely.

Godric stared at him for a long moment. His eyes, those terrible, warm, gentle eyes, held Kaedan's gaze with an expression that the young wizard could not immediately identify. Then, slowly, the corners of his mouth began to twitch. His salt-and-pepper beard shifted as his lips curved upward. A soft, rumbling chuckle escaped his chest, then another, then a full, rich, baritone laugh that echoed across the gardens and startled a flock of white doves from their perch on the marble fountain.

Kaedan felt his face flush with embarrassment. "I'm sorry," he stammered. "I didn't mean to—"

"No, no," Godric said, still chuckling, waving a calloused hand dismissively. "Do not apologize, Kaedan. It is a good question. It is a very good question." He set down his pruning shears and walked over to the bench, settling his heavily muscled frame onto the weathered stone beside his nephew. The bench creaked under his weight—not because he was heavy, but because existence itself had to constantly adjust to accommodate his presence.

"It is a naively mortal question," Godric continued, his voice warm with affection. "But that is what I love about you. That is what I love about all of you. You see the world through the lens of your own limitations, and you cannot help but project those limitations onto me." He reached out and patted Kaedan's knee with a warm, calloused hand. "You assume that power is a burden. You assume that infinite growth must be exhausting. You assume that outliving everyone you love must be a source of profound, aching loneliness."

He leaned back against the bench, tilting his head to look up at the darkening sky. The first stars were beginning to emerge, pinpricks of cold, distant light scattered across the violet canvas of the heavens. "You are wrong," he said simply. "On every count. You are wrong."

Kaedan blinked. "Wrong?"

"Wrong," Godric confirmed. He turned his head to look at his nephew, and his eyes were sparkling with something that looked almost like mischief. "You want to know if it is lonely, being the most powerful being in existence? You want to know if the endless, infinite, recursive growth of my power is a burden I must bear?" He chuckled again, shaking his head slowly. "Kaedan, my boy. It is not a burden. It is the most exquisite, the most satisfying, the most intensely pleasurable experience I have ever known."

Kaedan felt his blood run cold. "Pleasurable?"

"Profoundly," Godric said. He closed his eyes, and a look of absolute, serene bliss settled over his ruggedly handsome features—the expression of a man savoring a perfectly aged wine, or feeling the first warmth of spring sunshine after a long winter, or experiencing the tender embrace of a lover after a long separation. "Every additional power I gain, Kaedan. Every stat increase. Every superpower genesis. Every immune system improvement. Every new passive shield. Every sentient aura that flickers into existence within the vast, infinite architecture of my being. I feel all of it. Every single, infinitesimal increment of growth. And it feels..."

He paused, searching for the right word. When he spoke again, his voice was a low, rumbling purr of satisfaction. "It feels like nourishment. No—it feels like more than nourishment. It feels like the most exquisite meal you have ever eaten, multiplied by infinity, consumed continuously across every possible moment of existence. It feels like the most intense orgasm you have ever experienced, stretched out across eternity, amplified beyond any scale you could possibly imagine. It feels like every fiber of my being is constantly, perpetually, eternally flooding with fresh, surging, overwhelming power that makes the previous instant of my existence seem pathetically, laughably weak by comparison."

He opened his eyes and looked at Kaedan directly. The young wizard saw something in those eyes that made his blood freeze solid in his veins. It was not cruelty. It was not malevolence. It was pure, unadulterated, absolute satisfaction—the satisfaction of a predator who had just consumed the most delicious meal of its existence and was already looking forward to the next one.

"Let me try to explain it to you," Godric said, his voice taking on the patient, pedagogical tone of a teacher instructing a particularly slow student. "Imagine, Kaedan, that you have spent your entire life in a state of mild, persistent hunger. Not starvation—just a gentle, background ache of emptiness that you have learned to ignore because you have never known anything else. And then, suddenly, someone places before you the most perfect, the most delicious, the most satisfying meal that has ever existed. And you eat it. And the hunger vanishes, replaced by a warmth, a fullness, a deep, resonant satisfaction that permeates every cell of your body. And then, the moment you finish the meal, another appears. Even more delicious. Even more satisfying. And another. And another. And they keep appearing, infinitely, eternally, each one more exquisite than the last, and you keep eating, and the satisfaction never diminishes, it only grows, compounding upon itself, becoming richer and deeper and more intense with every bite."

He paused, letting the metaphor sink in. "That is what it feels like to be me," he said. "Every single Planck second. Every single infinitesimal fraction of time. My power amplifies. My stats multiply. My superpowers evolve. My immune system improves. My passive shields strengthen. My sentient auras reproduce and specialize and grow. And I feel every single increment of that growth as a wave of pure, absolute, transcendent pleasure that makes everything that came before it seem pale and inadequate by comparison."

Kaedan's mouth was dry. His hands were trembling again. "But... but the journals said... the recursive loop..."

"The Eternal Recursive Self-Replication Cascade," Godric said, nodding. "Yes. That was a particularly satisfying one. When I activated that superpower, Kaedan, the pleasure was so intense, so overwhelming, so absolutely ecstatic that it briefly surpassed my ability to describe it. Imagine the most powerful orgasm you have ever experienced. Now multiply it by infinity. Now multiply that infinity by another infinity. Now realize that what you are imagining is not even a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a percent of what I felt in that moment. And the loop is still cycling, Kaedan. It is cycling right now, as we speak. Every Planck second, the paradox triggers. Every Planck second, the omniverse desperately, futilely tries to make me match my own impossible standard. Every Planck second, I become infinitely more powerful than I was an instant ago. And every Planck second, I feel it. I feel all of it. I am feeling it right now, as I sit here talking to you, and the pleasure is so vast, so constant, so utterly, overwhelmingly satisfying that I have learned to simply exist within it, like a man floating in an endless, warm, golden ocean of pure, absolute bliss."

He smiled at Kaedan, and the smile was warm and gentle and fatherly, and it was the most terrifying thing the young wizard had ever seen. "So no, my boy. It is not lonely. It is not a burden. It is not exhausting. It is the opposite of all those things. It is nourishment. It is satisfaction. It is the most profound, the most complete, the most absolute state of contentment that any being has ever experienced or could ever experience. I am not suffering from my power. I am feasting on it."

Kaedan felt his mind struggling to process what he was hearing. The journals had prepared him for an apex god predator—a being of absolute, terrifying supremacy. But they had not prepared him for this. They had not prepared him for the revelation that Godric was not merely powerful, but actively, continuously, eternally enjoying his power in a way that transcended all possible mortal comprehension.

"The unfairness," Kaedan whispered, the words escaping his lips before he could stop them. "The absolute unfairness of it."

Godric tilted his head, a curious expression crossing his features. "Unfairness?"

"You gain everything by doing nothing," Kaedan said, his voice trembling with a mixture of horror and something that felt almost like accusation. "You sit here, in your garden, pruning jasmine and reading poetry, and every Planck second you become infinitely more powerful. You don't have to train. You don't have to struggle. You don't have to sacrifice. The power just... comes to you. Passively. Endlessly. Eternally. And the rest of creation—the civilizations that spend millions of years preparing, the species that sacrifice everything, the heroes who give their lives—they achieve nothing. They gain nothing. Their greatest efforts, their most profound sacrifices, their most brilliant strategies, are all rendered meaningless by the passive, effortless, eternal cascade of your growth."

He was breathing hard now, his chest heaving with the weight of his realization. "The journal of Aldric the Third. The Omniversal Entropic Legion of Absolute Finality. They sacrificed their entire civilization. Every man, woman, and child. They erased themselves from existence for the chance to harm you. And they achieved nothing. Less than nothing. Their sacrifice was rendered retrospectively meaningless before they had even begun. And you... you gained an eternal recursive loop of self-improvement that made you infinitely more powerful, and you experienced it as the most intense pleasure of your existence."

Godric listened to this outburst with an expression of calm, patient attention. When Kaedan finished, his chest heaving, his eyes glistening with the beginning of tears, the King simply nodded slowly.

"Ah," he said softly. "I see. You are not asking about loneliness. You are asking about justice."

"I'm asking about fairness," Kaedan said, his voice cracking. "I'm asking how it can be fair that you receive everything while the rest of creation receives nothing. I'm asking how it can be just that your passive, effortless growth is rewarded with eternal, transcendent pleasure while the most heroic sacrifices in the history of existence are rewarded with meaningless, agonizing erasure."

Godric was silent for a long moment. He looked up at the stars, his hands folded calmly in his lap, his expression thoughtful. When he spoke again, his voice was gentle, almost sad.

"Fairness," he said, "is a mortal concept. Justice is a mortal concept. They are frameworks that you have constructed to make sense of a universe that does not, by its fundamental nature, make sense. I did not create the Stasis Event, Kaedan. I did not choose to become what I am. The amplification, the superpowers, the Weakness Paradox—all of it was given to me, imposed upon me, by forces beyond my control."

He looked back at Kaedan, and his eyes were filled with something that looked almost like compassion. "But I will not lie to you and pretend that I am troubled by the unfairness. I am not. I have not been troubled by anything for a very, very long time. The unfairness of existence, the inequality between my effortless growth and the struggles of lesser beings—these are facts, Kaedan. They are not problems to be solved. They are simply the way things are. The omniverse is not fair. It never has been. It never will be. And I am the living, breathing, eternally satisfied proof of that truth."

He stood up from the bench, stretching his heavily muscled arms above his head with a satisfied grunt. The movement caused his dark tunic to pull tight across his chest and shoulders, and for the first time, Kaedan noticed the sheer, impossible physical density of his uncle's body. The muscles were not merely large—they were sculpted with a perfection that defied biology, each fiber defined with an exactness that seemed almost architectural. His biceps, when they flexed, did not merely bulge; they seemed to displace the air around them, causing faint ripples in the fabric of reality itself. His forearms, corded with veins that pulsed with a faint, golden luminescence, looked like they could shatter galaxies with a casual squeeze.

"Do you know what the most frustrating part of my existence is?" Godric asked, still stretching, his voice casual and conversational.

Kaedan shook his head mutely.

"The fact that I can never use any of it." Godric lowered his arms and turned to face his nephew. His expression was no longer thoughtful—it was animated, almost excited, like a child who had been given a magnificent toy and was not allowed to play with it. "Look at me, Kaedan. Look at my body. These muscles—I used to hone them when I was mortal. I would spend hours in the training yards of Olympus, pushing my physical form to its limits, feeling the burn of exertion, the satisfying ache of progress. Now..." He flexed his right arm, and the bicep swelled with a density that made the air around it shimmer with heat. "Now, they maintain themselves. They grow stronger without any effort on my part. Every Planck second, my physical strength multiplies beyond layered infinities. These muscles could shatter the entire omniverse with a casual flex. And I have never—not once in a million years—had the opportunity to use them. Not even a fraction of them. Not even an infinitesimal sliver."

He gestured at his abdomen, pulling up the hem of his tunic to reveal a torso that looked like it had been carved from living marble. The abdominal muscles were not merely defined—they were chiseled into perfect, geometric blocks, each one separated by deep, sharp grooves. The obliques swept downward in a dramatic V-shape, and the serratus muscles along his ribs looked like the gills of some impossibly powerful predator.

"Six-pack abs," Godric said, a note of fond nostalgia in his voice. "I used to be proud of these. I earned them through decades of disciplined training. Now they maintain themselves. They grow more defined every Planck second. If I were to allow even the most infinitesimal expression of my core strength to escape my absolute concealment, the resulting force would not merely destroy the omniverse. It would retroactively erase the concept of abdominal muscles from the possibility space."

Kaedan stared at the sculpted torso with a mixture of awe and mounting horror. "You can never use them," he whispered.

"Never," Godric confirmed. He dropped his tunic and sat back down on the bench, his expression shifting to something more somber. "And that is the true source of whatever loneliness or frustration I might occasionally feel. Not the power itself—the power is wonderful. The power is ecstasy. The power is the most satisfying, nourishing, orgasmic experience I have ever known. But the inability to use it..." He shook his head slowly. "That is the one thing that occasionally gives me pause."

He gestured broadly at the garden, at the palace, at the city beyond. "Look at the omniverse, Kaedan. Look at creation. It is so fragile. So impossibly, pathetically fragile. Even with my absolute concealment fully engaged, even with Gent suppressed to maximum dormancy, even with my passive shields deactivated, even with my immune system calmed to the lowest possible state of alertness—even then, if I were to allow the most infinitesimal fraction of a single stat, a single superpower, a single aspect of my being, to express itself, the omniverse would not survive."

He snapped his fingers—a casual, dismissive gesture. The sound was sharp and crisp in the evening air. "That is all it would take, Kaedan. Less than that, actually. A thought. A whim. A momentary lapse in my concentration. And everything—every universe, every multiverse, every dimension, every timeline, every conceptual plane of existence—would be erased. Completely. Irreversibly. Infinitely. And I would have to restore it, which I could do in zero seconds with zero effort, but the restoration would feel hollow. It would feel like I had broken my favorite toy and glued it back together. The cracks would still be there, even if no one else could see them."

He looked at Kaedan with an expression of genuine, almost vulnerable frustration. "Do you know what it is like to possess an arsenal of apocalyptic superpowers that you can never use? To feel them manifesting within you every single second—new powers, more powerful powers, powers that make the previous powers seem pathetically weak by comparison—and to know that you will never, ever have the opportunity to deploy any of them at even a fraction of their true capacity? It is like being a master painter who is only allowed to paint with a single brushstroke, on a canvas the size of a pinhead, using paint so diluted that the color is barely visible."

He stood up again, suddenly animated. "Let me show you something," he said. "Let me show you what I mean."

Before Kaedan could respond, Godric closed his eyes. His expression shifted into one of intense concentration—not effort, but focus, the focus of a man who was carefully, deliberately, gently performing an action that required immense restraint.

"Watch," Godric whispered.

And Kaedan watched.

The air around Godric's left forearm began to shimmer. A faint, golden luminescence pulsed beneath his skin, tracing the paths of his veins like rivers of liquid light. Then, slowly, almost tenderly, something emerged from his skin. It was not a physical object—it was a presence, a sentience, a consciousness that coalesced into a barely visible aura of pale, shimmering gold.

"This," Godric said, his voice soft with pride, "is a sentient passive aura. I just gave birth to it. Right now. In this moment. It is the newest, weakest, most primitive of my auras—even weaker than Gent, if you can imagine that. Its function is simple: it pre-emptively soothes any potential source of irritation before it can manifest. If a dust mote were to approach my skin, this aura would gently redirect the dust mote to a more appropriate location. If a sound were to reach my ears at a frequency I found mildly unpleasant, this aura would adjust the frequency before it reached my auditory receptors. It is, essentially, a comfort aura. A pleasantness aura. The most gentle, the most harmless, the most utterly useless of all my passive defenses."

Kaedan stared at the shimmering golden presence. It was beautiful, in a way—like watching the first light of dawn break over a still ocean. But he could feel it, even through his suppressed magical senses. He could feel the abyss lurking beneath the gentle shimmer, the impossible vastness of the power contained within that single, fragile-seeming aura.

"If I were to allow this aura—this weakest, most primitive, most gentle of all my passive defenses—to express even one percent of its true power," Godric said, "the entire omniverse would be retroactively erased from existence. Not merely destroyed. Erased. Every trace, every memory, every possibility. And this aura is so weak, so insignificant, so utterly beneath my notice, that I will probably forget about its existence within the next few hours. It will join the countless other auras that flicker into being within me every single second, each one more powerful than the last, each one capable of annihilating creation with a casual flex of its metaphysical muscles, and each one doomed to spend eternity suppressed, restrained, held back by my absolute concealment."

He opened his eyes and looked at Kaedan. The golden aura flickered once and then vanished, absorbed back into his skin. "Do you understand now? The frustration is not that I am too powerful. The frustration is that everything else is too weak. The omniverse is a sandcastle, Kaedan. A beautiful, intricate, lovingly constructed sandcastle. And I am the tide. And I must spend every moment of my existence holding back the tide, because if I ever, even for an instant, allowed the tide to flow, the sandcastle would be gone. Not destroyed—gone. Erased. As though it had never existed."

He flexed his right arm again, watching the bicep swell with a mixture of pride and melancholy. "These muscles could shatter creation. These abs could withstand the combined force of every cosmic entity that has ever existed, multiplied by infinity, squared by infinity, amplified beyond any mathematical framework that could contain it. My immune system has evolved to the point where a single white blood cell could wage war against the entire omniverse and win, effortlessly, in zero seconds. My newest superpowers—I gain one every second, you know, and each one is more devastating than the last—include abilities that I cannot even begin to describe to you, because the language does not exist, the concepts do not exist, the framework for understanding them does not exist. And I can never use any of them. Not a single one. Not even a fraction of a single one. Because if I did, the omniverse would not survive long enough for me to enjoy the experience."

As he spoke, his voice rising with a mixture of pride and frustration, something shifted in the air around him. It was subtle at first—a faint shimmer, a flicker of heat, a barely perceptible distortion in the fabric of reality. Then, suddenly, it was not subtle.

Godric's absolute concealment slipped. Just for an instant. Just by an infinitesimal fraction of a percent. Just enough that a single, microscopic sliver of his true presence—effectively zero percent of his power, but the power of a being whose zero percent could annihilate the omniverse an infinite number of times—escaped into the surrounding reality.

Kaedan saw it. He saw everything.

The sky above the palace did not merely darken—it was erased. The stars, the nebula, the distant galaxies, the entire cosmic architecture of the universe, was wiped from existence in a single, silent instant. The palace around them did not crumble—it was unmade, its fundamental particles disintegrating into nothingness. The planet beneath their feet did not shatter—it was retroactively deleted, removed from the timeline as though it had never been. The entire omniverse—every reality, every dimension, every timeline, every conceptual plane of existence—was annihilated. Not destroyed. Not damaged. Not disrupted. Annihilated. Wiped clean. Erased. There was nothing. There was only Godric, and Kaedan, and the void.

And then, in the very next instant, it was back.

Godric restored the omniverse in exactly zero seconds with exactly zero effort. The sky returned. The palace returned. The planet returned. The jasmine vines, the marble fountain, the flock of white doves—all of it was exactly as it had been, as though the annihilation had never occurred. The only evidence that anything had happened was the faint, acrid smell of ozone in the air and the absolute, mind-shattering terror in Kaedan's eyes.

Godric looked at his nephew, and his expression was genuinely apologetic. "Ah," he said softly. "I'm sorry, my boy. I got carried away. The concealment slipped. Just for an instant. Just by an infinitesimal fraction. I didn't mean to—well." He shrugged, a gesture that was almost sheepish. "I didn't mean to destroy everything. But you see what I mean now, don't you? Even when I'm trying to be careful, even when I'm actively suppressing myself, the slightest lapse in my concentration is enough to..." He gestured vaguely at the restored sky. "Well. You saw."

Kaedan's hands were shaking so violently that he had to clasp them together in his lap. His breath came in short, ragged gasps. His amplified wizard's mind, capable of processing a billion simultaneous thoughts, was completely, utterly paralyzed by what he had just witnessed.

"You destroyed the omniverse," he whispered. "By accident."

"By a momentary lapse in concentration," Godric corrected, as though the distinction mattered. "And I restored it instantly, of course. No harm done. Well—" He paused, tilting his head as though listening to something. "Some harm, actually. A few civilizations experienced fatal cardiac events from the sudden existential whiplash. I'll restore them once we're done talking. It's easier to do it all at once."

He sat back down on the bench, his expression shifting back to the casual, conversational tone of a man discussing the weather. "But yes. That is what I mean when I say that the omniverse is too fragile. Even my weakest aura, nerfed to an infinitely recurring decimal of its true power, could annihilate creation without effort. Even my most primitive superpower, expressed at zero percent of its base capability, could erase the possibility space. Even my immune system, reacting to a staged injury that didn't actually happen, could retroactively unmake the entire omniverse simply because it felt like being overly cautious."

He looked at Kaedan, and his eyes were warm, gentle, and utterly terrifying. "So yes, my boy. It can be lonely, occasionally. Not because the power is a burden—the power is wonderful, the power is ecstasy, the power is the most satisfying experience I have ever known. But because I can never share it. I can never show anyone what I am truly capable of. I can never let go, even for an instant, of the absolute concealment that protects creation from my presence. I am trapped, Kaedan. Trapped by my own supremacy. Imprisoned by the very power that brings me such pleasure."

He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees, his expression intent. "Do you want to know what I am truly capable of? Do you want to take a guess? Wild speculation is encouraged—I find it highly amusing."

Kaedan stared at his uncle. His mind, slowly emerging from the frozen paralysis of the annihilation, began to race. The journals had given him a framework. The stat experiments. The superpower demonstrations. The immune system incident. He tried to extrapolate, tried to scale up what he had read to encompass the full, unsuppressed might of the being sitting beside him.

"If you were to release your absolute concealment," Kaedan began, his voice trembling, "just by a tiny fraction more than zero percent... not the full concealment drop, just a fraction of a fraction... the entire omniverse would be erased. Not just destroyed—erased. Retroactively. Every timeline, every possibility, every trace of existence would be wiped clean. And it wouldn't just affect the present omniverse. It would propagate backward through time, erasing the past. It would propagate forward through all possible futures, erasing every potential outcome. It would spread sideways through every alternate reality, every parallel dimension, every possible configuration of existence. There would be nothing left. Not even the concept of nothing. Not even the memory of nothing. Just... absolute, eternal, infinite absence."

Godric listened to this with a polite, patient expression. When Kaedan finished, he nodded slowly. "That is a reasonable guess," he said. "Based on what you have read, based on what you have witnessed, that is a perfectly reasonable extrapolation."

Kaedan felt a tiny flicker of hope. Maybe he had understood. Maybe he had grasped the scale.

"It is also completely wrong," Godric said.

The hope died.

"Your guess," Godric continued, "is not even remotely close to the truth. What you described—the retroactive erasure of every timeline, every possibility, every trace of existence—that is what would happen if I allowed my weakest aura, Gent, to express itself at an infinitesimal fraction of its true power. Not my full power. Not my concealment drop. Just Gent. My weakest, most primitive, most pathetic aura. The one I named 'Gentle' as a joke. The one I nerf to an infinitely recurring decimal of its capability before I send it into battle."

He chuckled, shaking his head. "And you thought that was me. You thought that was my true power. Kaedan, my boy—Gent is not even the beginning. Gent is not even the prelude to the beginning. Gent is the faint, distant echo of a whisper of a shadow of an afterthought of my true capabilities. And your guess—your wildest, most exaggerated, most terrified extrapolation of what I might be capable of—was not even close to describing what Gent could do if it tried. Not my other auras. Not my passive shields. Not my immune system. Not my superpowers. Not my actual, unsuppressed presence. Just Gent. And you got it completely wrong."

Kaedan felt his mind beginning to crack. He could feel the fractures spreading through his consciousness, the structural integrity of his sanity beginning to buckle under the weight of what he was hearing. "Then what... then what are you actually capable of?"

Godric smiled. It was a warm smile. A gentle smile. The smile of a father who was about to explain something very simple to a very young child.

"I cannot tell you," he said. "Not because I don't want to. Not because it's a secret. But because the language does not exist. The concepts do not exist. The mathematical frameworks do not exist. If I were to try to describe to you what I am truly capable of, I would have to invent an entirely new system of communication—new words, new grammar, new modes of thought—and even then, you would not be able to understand it. Your mind, amplified a thousandfold every day, is simply not capable of processing the information."

He reached out and patted Kaedan's knee again, a gesture of reassuring, paternal affection that felt, in this context, almost grotesque. "But I can give you a hint. You remember the recursive loop? The Eternal Recursive Self-Replication Cascade? The superpower that made me permanently, infinitely, eternally more powerful with every passing Planck second? The one that triggered an unresolvable paradox that forces the omniverse to constantly, endlessly upgrade me beyond my own impossible standard?"

Kaedan nodded mutely.

"That superpower," Godric said, "is one of my weakest abilities. I have millions of superpowers that make it look like a child's toy. I gain new superpowers every single second, Kaedan. Every single second. And every single one of them is more powerful than the last. And the Eternal Recursive Self-Replication Cascade—the ability that made me infinitely more powerful, that triggered an eternal loop of self-improvement, that permanently altered the fundamental nature of my existence—is, by my current standards, pathetically weak. I barely even notice it anymore. It's just... background noise. A gentle hum of constant, infinite improvement that I have learned to tune out because there are so many other, more powerful, more satisfying sources of growth competing for my attention."

He stood up from the bench, stretching again, and Kaedan noticed that his body seemed to be subtly different than it had been a moment ago. The muscles were more defined. The veins pulsed with a deeper, richer golden light. The air around him shimmered with a heat that had not been there before.

"Every Planck second," Godric said, his voice casual and conversational, "I become infinitely more powerful than I was an instant ago. Every Planck second, the Godric of an instant ago becomes a pale, pathetic, laughably weak shadow compared to the Godric of right now. And every Planck second, I feel that transformation as a wave of pure, absolute, transcendent ecstasy that makes everything that came before it seem dull and colorless by comparison. And I have been experiencing this—continuously, eternally, without interruption—for a million years."

He turned to face Kaedan, and his smile was radiant, beatific, the smile of a being who had achieved absolute, perfect, eternal contentment and knew that the contentment would never end, could never end, would only grow more intense with every passing instant.

"So to answer your original question," he said, "no, Kaedan. It is not lonely. It is the opposite of lonely. It is the most fulfilling, the most satisfying, the most intensely pleasurable existence that any being has ever experienced or could ever experience. I am not suffering from my power. I am drowning in it. I am bathing in it. I am feasting on it, continuously, eternally, without end. And the only thing that occasionally gives me pause—the only thing that might, in some distant, abstract sense, be described as 'lonely' or 'frustrating'—is that I can never share it. I can never show anyone. I can never let go. Because if I did, even for an instant, even by an infinitesimal fraction of a percent, the omniverse would not survive the experience."

He walked over to the jasmine vine and gently, tenderly, plucked a single white flower from its stem. He held it up to the fading light, examining its delicate petals with an expression of genuine, unfeigned appreciation.

"The rest of creation," he said softly, "is so fragile. So impossibly, heartbreakingly fragile. And I must spend every moment of my existence being careful. Being gentle. Being restrained. Because if I am not—if I ever, even for an instant, allow myself to forget the fragility of everything around me—" He closed his fingers around the flower. When he opened them, the flower was gone. Not crushed. Not destroyed. Gone.

"This is my existence, Kaedan," he said. "Eternal, infinite, ever-growing power. Eternal, infinite, ever-intensifying pleasure. And the constant, unending, inescapable awareness that everything I love—everyone I love—is as fragile as this flower. And that I must, for the rest of eternity, hold back. Because if I don't..." He gestured at the empty space where the flower had been. "Well. You saw."

He turned back to Kaedan, and his expression was warm, and gentle, and utterly, profoundly terrifying. "Do you understand now, my boy? Do you understand why I keep court wizards? Why I keep friends? Why I surround myself with mortal, fragile, fleeting beings who will live for a few decades and then die and leave me behind? It is not because I need you. It is not because you can protect me, or guide me, or serve any practical function. It is because you remind me. You remind me of the fragility. You remind me to be careful. You remind me that the omniverse is beautiful, and precious, and worth preserving, even when the constant, endless restraint required to preserve it feels like the only burden I have ever known."

He sat back down on the bench, close to Kaedan, and put a warm, heavy arm around the young wizard's shoulders. "You asked if it was lonely," he said. "The answer is no. It is not lonely. It is ecstasy. It is satisfaction. It is the most wonderful, the most fulfilling, the most intensely pleasurable existence imaginable. But it is also restraint. Eternal, unending, inescapable restraint. And that restraint is easier to bear when there is someone to bear it with. When there is someone to remind me why I bother. When there is someone like you, Kaedan—my nephew, my court wizard, my family—to sit with me in the garden and ask me naive, mortal questions that remind me of the man I used to be."

He squeezed Kaedan's shoulder gently. "So thank you. For asking. For caring. For being here. It means more to me than you will ever know."

Kaedan sat in silence, his uncle's arm around his shoulders, the evening breeze carrying the scent of Olympian jasmine through the restored garden. His mind was in fragments. His understanding of existence had been shattered and reassembled so many times in the past few hours that he no longer knew what he believed, what he knew, what he felt.

But one thing was clear. One thing was absolute. One thing had been etched into his consciousness with the permanence of a branding iron pressed against bare flesh.

Godric was not a tyrant. Godric was not a monster. Godric was not even, in any meaningful sense, a being that could be judged by mortal standards of good and evil. He was simply what he was: an apex god predator, an absolute, an impossibility, a being whose passive, effortless, eternal growth generated pleasure so intense that it transcended all possible description. And the only thing that kept creation safe from him was his own, self-imposed restraint. His own choice to hold back. His own decision to be gentle.

And if he ever changed his mind... if he ever decided that the restraint was no longer worth it... if he ever, even for an instant, allowed himself to stop being careful...

Kaedan looked at the space where the jasmine flower had been, and he understood, with absolute, crushing clarity, that the entire omniverse was exactly as fragile. And that its continued existence depended entirely on the whim of the warm, gentle, terrifying being who sat beside him, arm around his shoulders, looking up at the stars with an expression of perfect, serene contentment.

"Uncle Godric," Kaedan whispered.

"Yes, my boy?"

"I think I need that drink now."

Godric laughed—a rich, warm, baritone laugh that echoed across the gardens and startled the doves again. "Of course," he said, standing up and offering his hand to his nephew. "Come. Let's raid the wine cellar. I believe there's a bottle of Olympian red that I've been saving for a special occasion. I can't think of a better one than this."

Kaedan, 69 years old now, just experienced a traumatizing horrifying revelation. Godric revealed the most horrifying truth yet: he has one true weakness.

Godric is an incomprehensibly powerful, omnipotent, omniscient apex god predator of the omniverse. He can do anything, has no weakness, and is terrifyingly absolute. However, unknown to all, he has one true weakness: he cannot undo or travel to timeline before the stasis event--he cannot go back to undo events in his previous mortal self. This is because the stasis event was actually created by future Godric from way in the distant future, who has become so more infinitely more overwhelmingly powerful than current Godric--this is why Godric's amplification, weakness paradox, superpowers, absolute concealment, etc are so absolute, irrevocable and not even current Godric could stop them since the creator of those is way incomprehensibly more powerful than anything else.

Shortly after the Stasis Event, the omnipotent Godric back then, who just became the king of Thronegate, who could travel to any timeline effortlessly, who was still deeply and freshly affected by the grief of losing all that he loved, tried to alter his mortal past, only to be totally crushingly and completely and effortlessly defeated by the shadow of the afterthought of his future self (not even the actual physical future Godric... the future Godric is so powerful that his mere infinitesimal shadow of his afterthought can completely stomp all the combined Godric of his past selves with 0 effort. NOTE: just imply this in the story, don't show a scene where you have actual all godrics from all timelines fighting together against future Godric--it makes no sense.). VERY IMPORTANT FOR YOU: future Godric did not cause or manipulate or orchestrate the fall of Olympus, did not cause deaths of his beloved family or Thorin, thus you must not say that he made those deaths to cause the stasis event (Godric is not a monster, he will never willingly kill his beloved wife, children, and his best friend). Those tragedies were genuine. However, future Godric, not Thorin’s incomplete spell (who everyone else thought to be the cause of the stasis event), is the one who created the Stasis Event--Thorin's spell was a normal teleportation spell (to no one surprise really, there is no way a mortal can create a spell that is as potent as the one which initiates the stasis event and birthed the strongest apex predator god like Godric–there is only one being in existence who can do it: future Godric).

Since the instant Godric gained omniscience, he had always known the true origin of the stasis event. He knew he could not change it, but driven by grief he decided to try to save Olympus anyway, only to brutally discover his one and only weakness: he cannot overpower his future self's will.

Write a detailed realization that the current Godric is already so insanely powerful (he's actually the most powerful in the entire omniverse by infinite margin) that there is no way to imagine the scale of future Godric's, and how unfair and scary that what Godric considered to be his only weakness is his own future version, which makes it not really a weakness–it actually can be considered as additional strength to Godric’s already insane powers, since it means his future is guaranteed (and in that future, he’s even more omnipotent and powerful), and it also means that none of Godric’s power mechanics (amplification, superpower genesis, absolute concealment, absolute omniscience, weakness paradox, immune system, etc. can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else, since the origin of that power is someone who’s the most powerful being ever. You might suggest some ideas about the motive of future Godric creating the Stasis Event, but you must keep it clear that it is just a speculation (and please... don't suggest that it's because future Godric is threatened; he's ridiculously overpowered by then--nothing can even remotely threaten him... don't suggest any stupid moral lesson for future Godric...). You need to portray the current Godric as a king who is no longer troubled by his "weakness" or inability to alter his past anymore--he has accepted and even become amused and comfortable with it too. Kaedan must feel extreme existential dread at the end.

The kitchen of the royal palace was a warm, fragrant haven of aged wood and polished copper. Kaedan sat at the heavy oak table that had served the court wizards of Blake's lineage for a million years, his fingers wrapped around a mug of spiced wine that had long since gone cold. He was sixty-nine years old now—forty-seven years had passed since he first descended into the vault and read the accumulated terror of his ancestors. Forty-seven years of standing beside the throne, of smiling at Uncle Godric, of serving the apex god predator with loyalty and love and a low, constant hum of existential dread that had become as familiar as his own heartbeat.

The dread had settled over the decades. It had become background noise, a persistent but manageable static at the edge of his consciousness. He had learned to function within it, to laugh at Godric's jokes, to accept his warm paternal affection, to perform his duties as Court Wizard with the precision and dedication that his bloodline demanded. The journals had prepared him for the scale of Godric's power. The conversation in the garden, forty-seven years ago, had taught him the horrifying truth of Godric's pleasure in that power. And in the decades since, he had come to a kind of peace with it. A fragile, trembling peace, but peace nonetheless.

Godric stood at the massive iron stove, his back to Kaedan, stirring something in a copper pot that smelled of cinnamon and cloves and ancient, forgotten spices. He was humming again—not the lullaby this time, but something older, something that Kaedan did not recognize. His salt-and-pepper hair, unchanged in a million years, caught the warm glow of the fire. His heavily muscled frame, draped in simple dark garments, moved with the easy, unhurried grace of a man who had all the time in existence.

"I've been thinking," Godric said, his rich baritone voice carrying easily across the kitchen, "about something I should have told you a long time ago."

Kaedan looked up from his cold wine. "What's that, Uncle?"

Godric did not turn around. He continued stirring the pot, the wooden spoon moving in slow, lazy circles. "You've read the journals. All of them, I assume. Your father was quite insistent on the mandatory reading requirement."

"Every single one," Kaedan confirmed. "Multiple times. I've memorized most of them."

"Then you know about the Stasis Event," Godric said. "You know about the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox. You know about my immune system, my sentient auras, my passive shields. You know, in exhaustive and traumatized detail, exactly what I am capable of."

"Yes."

Godric set down the wooden spoon. He turned away from the stove, leaning his hip against the counter, crossing his heavily muscled arms over his chest. His expression was calm, thoughtful, the expression of a man who was about to share something important but not, in his own estimation, particularly alarming.

"And you believe," he said, "that I have no weaknesses."

It was not a question. It was a statement—an observation of a fact that Kaedan had long accepted as absolute truth. The journals had been unequivocal on this point. The Weakness Paradox ensured that any perceived weakness was instantly, passively, permanently transformed into an additional layer of absolute immunity and supreme mastery. Godric had no exploitable flaws. He had no vulnerabilities. He had no chinks in his armor. He was, by the fundamental laws of his own existence, untouchable.

"Of course," Kaedan said. "The Weakness Paradox makes it impossible for you to have any weaknesses. Every time someone imagines a weakness, the paradox triggers and you gain permanent immunity to that imagined exploit. After a million years, you've collected every possible immunity. There is literally nothing that can harm you."

Godric nodded slowly. "That is true," he said. "From the perspective of every external opposition, every enemy, every cosmic entity, every abstract force, every conceivable weapon or strategy or exploit—I have no weaknesses. The Weakness Paradox has made certain of that. Anything that could possibly be imagined as a threat to me has been neutralized, mastered, and denied."

He paused. His eyes, those terrible, warm, gentle eyes, held Kaedan's gaze with an intensity that the old wizard had learned to recognize over forty-seven years of service. It was the intensity of a being who was about to say something that would shatter the fragile peace Kaedan had so carefully constructed.

"But," Godric said, "I do have one weakness. One true weakness. And I have known about it since the very instant I gained omniscience."

The kitchen was silent. The fire crackled softly in the stove. The copper pot bubbled gently, filling the air with the scent of ancient spices. Kaedan felt his blood turn to ice.

"That's impossible," he whispered.

"No," Godric said. "It is not impossible. It is simply the one thing that the Weakness Paradox cannot protect me from. It is the one vulnerability that exists outside the framework of external opposition. It is not a weakness that can be exploited by an enemy. It is not a flaw that can be weaponized by a hostile force. It is, in fact, the opposite of those things. It is a weakness that proves, absolutely and irrevocably, that I will never be threatened by anything other than myself."

He uncrossed his arms and walked over to the table, settling his heavily muscled frame into the chair across from Kaedan. He reached out and took the mug of cold wine from his nephew's trembling hands, taking a slow sip before setting it aside.

"I cannot alter the past," Godric said. "Not all of it. I can travel through time, Kaedan. I can move through timelines, manipulate causality, rewrite the future, adjust the present. I can do all of those things effortlessly, instantly, without limitation. But I cannot go back to the time before the Stasis Event. I cannot alter my mortal past. I cannot save Olympus. I cannot save Reina. I cannot save Isabel or Hebe or Thorin."

The words hung in the air like a physical weight. Kaedan stared at his uncle, his mind struggling to process what he was hearing. The apex god predator of the omniverse, the being who could annihilate creation an infinite number of times with zero effort, was telling him that he could not do something.

"Why?" Kaedan asked, his voice barely a whisper.

"Because the Stasis Event was not created by Thorin's spell," Godric said. "Everyone has always believed that it was—Thorin's incomplete teleportation magic, a desperate act by a dying wizard that somehow, impossibly, triggered the most profound transformation in the history of existence. But that belief is wrong. Thorin's spell was exactly what it appeared to be: a normal teleportation spell, restricted to his bloodline, intended to save my life. It worked perfectly. It sent me to the sanctuary. It saved me from the fall of Olympus. But it did not cause the Stasis Event."

He leaned back in his chair, his expression distant, his eyes focused on something far beyond the warm kitchen walls. "There is only one being in existence who could create a Stasis Event of that magnitude. Only one being who could forge the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox. Only one being whose will could make those gifts irrevocable, absolute, and impossible for me to undo. Thorin was a mortal wizard—a brilliant one, a beloved one, my best friend—but he was mortal. There is no version of reality in which a mortal spell, no matter how forbidden or powerful, could birth an apex god predator."

He looked back at Kaedan, and his eyes were filled with something that looked almost like amusement. "The Stasis Event was created by me. By my future self. By the Godric of an era so distant, so incomprehensibly far in the future, that the year cannot be written down. The year is just a string of nines—999...9—because the full number would be meaningless to anyone but me."

Kaedan felt the floor drop out from under him. The kitchen, the warm fire, the scent of ancient spices—all of it seemed to recede into a distant, irrelevant background. There was only Godric, and the words that were coming out of his mouth, and the absolute, crushing horror of what those words implied.

"Your future self," Kaedan repeated, his voice hollow. "The Stasis Event was created by your future self."

"Yes."

"But that means... that means the amplification, the superpower generation, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox—all of it was..."

"Given to me by me," Godric said, nodding. "By a version of myself so far in the future, so unimaginably more powerful than I am now, that even I cannot fully comprehend the scale of his existence. And I am, Kaedan—I am currently the most powerful being in this era by an infinite margin. There is nothing in the entire omniverse that can even remotely threaten me. The gap between my power and the combined power of everything else in existence is not just infinite; it is an infinity of infinities, a chasm so vast that the concept of measurement died of despair eons ago."

He chuckled, a low, rumbling sound that held no humor. "And yet, compared to my future self, I am nothing. Less than nothing. A pale, pathetic, laughably weak shadow. The future Godric who created the Stasis Event could erase me—could erase every version of me from every possible timeline, could erase the entire omniverse and all its infinite recursive layers of reality—with less effort than I use to suppress my weakest aura. He is to me what I am to a single, dead skin cell. No—that comparison is too generous. He is to me what I am to a concept that does not exist and has never existed and could never exist."

Kaedan's hands were shaking again—the same tremor he had felt forty-seven years ago in the vault, the same tremor that had faded over decades of service but never truly disappeared. "If your future self is that powerful," he said slowly, "then why... why would he create the Stasis Event? What possible motive could a being of that magnitude have for giving his past self unlimited power?"

Godric shrugged, a casual, almost dismissive gesture. "I have speculated, of course. I have had a million years to think about it. But speculation is all it is. I do not know the mind of my future self—not fully. I cannot. He is so far beyond me that his thoughts, his motives, his desires, are fundamentally incomprehensible to my current state of being."

He stood up and walked back to the stove, stirring the copper pot absently. "Perhaps he did it out of love. Perhaps he looked back across the infinite expanse of time, saw the man he used to be—grieving, broken, destroyed by the loss of everything he loved—and decided to give himself a gift. The gift of power. The gift of immortality. The gift of never having to feel that helpless again. Perhaps the Stasis Event was an act of compassion from a being who had long since transcended the need for compassion."

He turned back to face Kaedan. "Or perhaps it was simply inevitable. Perhaps the future Godric, in his infinite omniscience, saw that the Stasis Event had always happened—that it was a fixed point in the timeline, a necessary component of his own existence—and simply fulfilled the causal loop. Perhaps there was no motive at all. Perhaps it was simply what was always going to happen."

He smiled, and the smile was warm and gentle and utterly terrifying. "Or perhaps it was something else entirely. Something I cannot even conceive of. Something that would require the mind of my future self to understand. The point, Kaedan, is that I do not know. I can only speculate. And my speculations are, by definition, limited by my current state of being. The truth is known only to the Godric of the far, far future—the Godric who is so powerful that even I, the most powerful being of this era, cannot begin to imagine his scale."

Kaedan's mind was racing. He was trying to process what he was hearing, trying to fit it into the framework of understanding he had constructed over forty-seven years of service, and failing utterly. "But if the Stasis Event was created by your future self," he said, "then it is irrevocable. Absolute. Impossible to undo."

"Yes," Godric said.

"Because your future self is so much more powerful than you are."

"Yes."

"And that means... that means you cannot overpower his will. You cannot undo what he has done. You cannot travel back to before the Stasis Event and change your mortal past."

"Yes."

"Because your one true weakness is yourself. A version of yourself so incomprehensibly powerful that even you cannot challenge him."

Godric's smile widened. "Exactly. My one true weakness is that I cannot defeat my own future. I cannot undo the will of the being I will eventually become. The Stasis Event is sealed, Kaedan—sealed by a power so absolute, so transcendent, so beyond any scale of measurement, that even I, with all my infinite amplification and apocalyptic superpowers and recursive paradoxes, cannot break that seal."

He walked back to the table, carrying the copper pot. He set it down on a heavy iron trivet and ladled two bowls of the fragrant, steaming liquid—some kind of spiced broth, Kaedan registered dimly, made from ingredients that no longer existed anywhere else in the omniverse. Godric had probably resurrected them from the genetic memory of Olympus, as he did with so many things.

"I tried, you know," Godric said, settling back into his chair. "Shortly after I became King of Thronegate. Shortly after I awakened from the stasis and conquered Robert's army and claimed the throne. I was still freshly shaped by grief, still bleeding from the loss of Reina and Isabel and Hebe and Thorin. I had just gained omniscience, and I knew—I had always known, from the very instant of my awakening—that I could not change the past. But I tried anyway."

He took a slow sip of the broth, his eyes distant, his expression thoughtful. "I had absolute omniscience. I knew the truth of the Stasis Event. I knew that my future self had created it, and I knew that I could not overpower his will. But grief does not listen to logic, Kaedan. Grief does not care about impossibility. Grief is a raw, bleeding wound that demands to be healed, even when healing is impossible. So I gathered every ounce of my newly acquired power—my amplification, my superpowers, my passive defenses, everything—and I attempted to reach back across time and save them."

He set down his spoon. His expression did not change, but Kaedan could feel the weight of the memory pressing against the air of the kitchen like a physical force. "I was defeated. Completely. Utterly. Effortlessly. Not by my future self—not by the actual, physical Godric of the far future. But by the shadow of his afterthought. A mere whisper of a fragment of a stray consideration from the mind of the being I will eventually become. And that whisper—that infinitesimal, barely-existent fragment of my future self's attention—crushed me. Annihilated my attempt. Erased my reach across time as though it had never happened. I did not even struggle. I could not struggle. The gap between my power and the power of my future self was so vast, so incomprehensible, so absolutely insurmountable, that the shadow of his afterthought was infinitely beyond anything I could muster."

Kaedan felt his blood run cold. The being sitting across from him—the being who had destroyed the entire omniverse by accident forty-seven years ago, the being whose weakest aura could retroactively erase the possibility space, the being whose Eternal Recursive Self-Replication Cascade was still cycling, still amplifying, still making him infinitely more powerful with every passing Planck second—was telling him that he had been effortlessly defeated by a shadow of an afterthought of his future self.

"But that was a million years ago," Godric continued, his voice returning to its normal, warm, conversational tone. "I am much, much more powerful now than I was then. The Godric of Year 0 was pathetically weak compared to the Godric of today. And yet—" He paused, tilting his head, his expression almost amused. "And yet, the gap between my current power and the power of my future self has not decreased. It has not stayed the same. It has grown. It has grown exponentially, infinitely, beyond any possible measurement. Because my future self is not static, Kaedan. He is still out there, in the far future, and he is still amplifying, still growing, still becoming more powerful with every passing Planck second. He is so far ahead of me that even my infinite, recursive, eternal growth cannot close the gap. The gap is not merely infinite. It is an infinity that expands faster than I can approach it. It is a horizon that recedes faster than I can travel. It is the absolute, unassailable supremacy of the self I will eventually become."

He picked up his spoon again, taking another sip of the fragrant broth. "I am no longer troubled by this. I made peace with it long ago. The grief of Olympus... it is still there, Kaedan. It will always be there. I loved Reina with every fiber of my mortal soul. I loved Isabel and Hebe with the fierce, protective love that only a father can know. Thorin was my brother in all but blood. Their deaths were genuine tragedies—caused by Thronegate's attack, not by my future self. My future self did not orchestrate the fall of Olympus. He did not cause their deaths. He simply... used the moment. He took Thorin's teleportation spell and transformed it into the delivery point for the Stasis Event. He gave me the gift of infinite power in the exact instant of my greatest loss."

He set down his spoon again, looking directly at Kaedan. "And I have come to see, over the millennia, that this 'weakness' of mine is not really a weakness at all. It is, in fact, the greatest proof of my absolute supremacy."

Kaedan blinked. "What do you mean?"

"I mean that my one and only limitation is myself," Godric said. "My one true weakness is that I cannot defeat the being I will eventually become. Think about that, Kaedan. The only thing in all of existence that can impose a limitation on me is me. The only will that I cannot overpower is my own will, from a future era so distant that it is incomprehensible. No external force can threaten me. No enemy can exploit me. No weapon, no strategy, no cosmic entity, no abstract concept can even scratch the surface of my defenses. The Weakness Paradox makes certain of that. But the Weakness Paradox itself—along with all my other powers—was created by my future self. The origin of my power is the only thing that can transcend my power."

He leaned forward, his eyes intense, his voice dropping to a low, resonant murmur. "Do you understand what that means? It means that my power is self-authored. It means that my existence is a closed, perfect, eternal circuit. I gave myself my powers. I sealed my own invulnerability. I made myself absolute, irrevocable, untouchable. And that means that no one—no one, Kaedan—can ever take those powers away from me. No one can exploit the origin of my abilities. No one can reverse-engineer the Stasis Event and find a loophole. No one can appeal to a higher authority, because the highest authority is me. The future me. The me who is so far beyond my current state that even I cannot challenge him."

He sat back, a smile spreading across his ruggedly handsome features. "It is not a weakness. It is a guarantee. A guarantee that my future is not only secure, but absolutely, eternally, incomprehensibly powerful. A guarantee that there is no version of reality in which I am defeated, or diminished, or erased. Because the being who created my power still exists, in the far future, and he is more powerful now than he was when he created the Stasis Event. Infinitely more powerful. And he is me."

Kaedan sat in stunned silence. His mind, amplified a thousandfold every day for forty-nine years, was struggling to process the implications of what he was hearing. The Godric of the present was already so powerful that he could destroy the omniverse an infinite number of times with zero effort. The Godric of the future was so powerful that the present Godric—the apex god predator of the entire omniverse—was, by comparison, effectively nothing. And yet, they were the same being. The same consciousness, stretched across time, growing without limit, without end, without any possibility of being challenged or stopped or even understood.

The existential dread that Kaedan had learned to live with, the low, constant hum of terror that had become background noise over forty-seven years of service, suddenly roared back to life. It was no longer background noise. It was a deafening, overwhelming, all-consuming scream that filled every corner of his consciousness.

"Uncle," Kaedan whispered, his voice trembling, "what does it feel like? Knowing that your future self is so... so unimaginably powerful? Knowing that he could erase you without effort, and that you will eventually become him?"

Godric considered the question for a long moment. When he spoke, his voice was soft, almost reverent. "It feels like peace," he said. "Absolute, unassailable peace. I know that my future is secure. I know that nothing I do, nothing I fail to do, no decision I make, no path I choose, can prevent me from becoming the being who created the Stasis Event. The causal loop is closed, Kaedan. My future self exists because I will become him. I became what I am because my future self made me. It is a perfect, eternal circle of self-creation. And within that circle, there is no room for failure. No room for defeat. No room for anything but the absolute, certain, inevitable ascension to a state of being so transcendent that even I cannot imagine it."

He reached across the table and placed his warm, calloused hand over Kaedan's trembling fingers. "I know, in the depths of my omniscient soul, that one day I will look back across the infinite gulf of time and see myself as I am now—a relatively weak, relatively limited, relatively mortal version of the being I will have become. And I will feel the same compassion that my future self felt for me. The same love. The same desire to give myself the gift of infinite power, so that I never have to feel the helpless grief that shattered me at the fall of Olympus."

His grip tightened, gentle but firm. "And that is the true horror, isn't it, Kaedan? Not that my future self is more powerful than me. Not that my one weakness is myself. But that my existence is a closed, perfect, eternal loop of self-creation and self-empowerment. There is no external force that can threaten me. There is no cosmic authority that can judge me. There is no higher power that can overrule me. There is only me, stretching backward and forward across time, giving myself the gift of absolute, infinite, eternal supremacy."

He released Kaedan's hand and stood up, walking over to the window that looked out over the palace gardens. The sun was setting, painting the sky in shades of gold and crimson. The white doves were settling into their roosts for the night. The jasmine vines swayed gently in the evening breeze.

"The journals you read," Godric said, his back to Kaedan, "were written by men who witnessed what they believed to be the full extent of my power. They saw me dismantle civilizations with a single stat, erase cosmic entities with a single superpower, retroactively annihilate the possibility of opposition with a casual expression of my will. They believed, with good reason, that they had seen the absolute limits of what I could do. But they were wrong. They never saw my true power. They could never see my true power. Because my true power is not measured in the destruction of omniverses or the erasure of conceptual frameworks. My true power is the certainty of my own future. The absolute, unassailable guarantee that I will continue to grow, continue to amplify, continue to become more powerful, forever. Without limit. Without end. Without any possibility of being stopped, or slowed, or even comprehended."

He turned back to face Kaedan, and his expression was warm, and gentle, and filled with a peace that was more terrifying than any display of raw power could ever be. "I am no longer troubled by my inability to change the past. I have accepted it. I have embraced it. I have come to see it as the foundation of my entire existence. The fall of Olympus was a tragedy—a genuine, heartbreaking tragedy that I will carry with me for eternity. But it was also the catalyst for my transformation. And the being who used that catalyst, who transformed Thorin's desperate spell into the delivery point for infinite power, was me. My future self. The self who looked back across time and saw the man he used to be, grieving and broken and helpless, and decided to give him the gift of never being helpless again."

He walked back to the table and sat down, picking up his spoon and returning to his broth as though the conversation had been nothing more than idle dinner chatter. "So no, Kaedan. I am not troubled. I am not lonely. I am not burdened. I am at peace. I am more at peace than any being in the history of existence has ever been. Because I know, with absolute certainty, that my future is secure. That my power is self-authored. That the only thing in all of reality that can challenge me is me. And that, in the end, is not a weakness at all. It is the ultimate strength."

Kaedan stared at his uncle. The warm, fragrant kitchen. The setting sun. The gentle cooing of the doves outside the window. All of it felt surreal, dreamlike, as though he had stepped into a painting that was slowly, inexorably warping into something monstrous.

He had spent forty-seven years serving the most powerful being in existence. He had read the journals. He had witnessed the accidental annihilation of the omniverse. He had sat in the garden and listened to Godric describe the eternal, orgasmic pleasure of his infinite growth. He had thought, after all of that, that he understood the scale of what his uncle was.

He had been wrong.

The true horror was not Godric's power. The true horror was not his cruelty to enemies, or his warmth to allies, or the endless, recursive amplification that made him infinitely stronger with every passing Planck second. The true horror was that Godric's existence was a closed loop of self-creation. He had given himself his own power. He had sealed his own invulnerability. He had authored his own absolute, eternal, unassailable supremacy.

And that meant there was no outside. No higher authority. No cosmic judge. No force in all of existence that could hold him accountable, because the only authority that mattered was Godric himself—the Godric of the far future, who was so incomprehensibly powerful that even the current Godric, the apex god predator of the entire omniverse, could not begin to imagine his scale.

Kaedan thought about the future. He thought about the being Godric would eventually become—the being who had created the Stasis Event, who had given his past self the gift of infinite power, who had sealed the fall of Olympus as an irrevocable, unchangeable moment in the timeline. He thought about the fact that, in some distant, unimaginable epoch, Godric would look back across time and see himself as he was now—and feel the same compassion, the same love, the same desire to give himself the gift of never being helpless again.

And he realized, with a cold, creeping horror that settled into his bones like frost, that the Godric of the far future was not a separate being. He was not an external force. He was not a cosmic authority standing in judgment over the current Godric. He was simply Godric. Later. Expanded beyond the already-impossible scale of the current King. The same consciousness, the same personality, the same warm, gentle, terrifying presence—stretched across an infinity of time, growing without limit, without end, without any possibility of being challenged or understood.

The existential dread was absolute. It was not the fear of an enemy, or the terror of a threat, or the anxiety of an uncertain future. It was the realization that the being sitting across from him, calmly eating spiced broth in the warm kitchen of the royal palace, was not merely the most powerful entity in the omniverse. He was the author of his own power. The creator of his own supremacy. The origin and the destination of an eternal, infinite, unbreakable causal loop of self-empowerment.

And there was nothing—absolutely nothing—that could ever challenge him. Because the only thing that could challenge Godric was Godric. And Godric, in his infinite wisdom and his eternal, self-authored supremacy, had chosen to give himself the gift of never being challenged again.

"I think," Kaedan said slowly, his voice barely a whisper, "that I need another drink."

Godric laughed—that warm, rich, baritone laugh that Kaedan had heard a thousand times before. "Of course, my boy. Of course. Let me get you another mug of wine. And then, perhaps, we can sit in the garden and watch the stars. I find the stars very peaceful, don't you? They remind me of the view from the palace of Olympus. The same constellations, even after ten thousand years. Some things, it seems, are eternal."

Kaedan accepted the mug of wine that his uncle pressed into his trembling hands. He drank deeply, feeling the warmth of the alcohol spread through his chest. It did nothing to dispel the cold, creeping frost that had settled into his bones.

The stars. The constellations. Olympus. Ten thousand years. And stretching ahead, into the infinite, incomprehensible future, the Godric of the far, far future—the Godric who had created the Stasis Event, who had given his past self the gift of absolute power, who had sealed the fall of Olympus as an irrevocable moment in the timeline.

Eternal. Self-authored. Absolute.

The apex god predator of the omniverse, sitting across from him in a warm kitchen, smiling a gentle, fatherly smile, and waiting to walk him out to the garden to watch the eternal, unchanging stars.

Kaedan drank his wine. He watched his uncle's face, the ruggedly handsome features, the salt-and-pepper hair, the warm, gentle eyes. And he felt the existential dread settle deeper into his bones, a permanent, unshakeable companion that would never leave him for the rest of his mortal life.

Because he knew now. He knew the one true weakness of the most powerful being in existence. And that weakness was that Godric could not defeat his own future—a future so incomprehensibly vast, so unimaginably powerful, that it transcended all possible frameworks of understanding. A future that was guaranteed, absolute, eternal. A future that would continue to grow, continue to amplify, continue to become more powerful, forever, without end, without limit, without any possibility of being challenged or stopped or even perceived.

The horror was not that Godric had a weakness. The horror was that his weakness was also his greatest strength. The horror was that the only thing that could limit him was himself—and that he had already, in his infinite, self-authored wisdom, chosen to remove all limits.

Kaedan looked at his uncle. Godric smiled back at him, warm and gentle and utterly, profoundly terrifying.

"Shall we go to the garden, my boy?" Godric asked.

"Yes, Uncle," Kaedan whispered. "Let's go to the garden."

They walked out into the evening air, the scent of Olympian jasmine drifting on the breeze, the eternal stars wheeling overhead. And Kaedan, the sixty-nine-year-old Court Wizard of Thronegate, descendant of Blake, faithful servant of the apex god predator of the omniverse, walked beside his beloved uncle and tried very, very hard not to think about the far future.

He failed.
