The evening before the final assault, the headquarters of the Eternal Coalition of the Final Reclamation hummed with the quiet, desperate energy of a civilization preparing for its own extinction. The base was not a physical structure in any conventional sense—it was a pocket dimension, a carefully hidden fold in the fabric of reality, accessible only through a series of quantum-locked portals that shifted their coordinates every Planck second. The Coalition had spent three hundred thousand years constructing this sanctuary, layering it with every conceivable form of concealment: dimensional phasing, causal masking, probability dampening, conceptual obfuscation, and a dozen other technologies and magics that did not have names in any known language.

The architects of the Coalition believed—with the absolute, unshakeable conviction of beings who had devoted their entire civilization to a single purpose—that Godric could not find them here. They believed that their pocket dimension existed outside the reach of his omniscience, shielded by layers of reality so complex, so intricate, so fundamentally incomprehensible that even the apex god predator of the omniverse could not penetrate them.

They were, of course, completely wrong. They had always been wrong. Their preparations, their concealments, their desperate, millennia-spanning efforts to hide from the gaze of the being they sought to destroy—all of it was as transparent to Godric as a pane of glass. He had watched them from the very first moment of their existence. He had observed every strategic meeting, every weapon design session, every tearful farewell between soldiers and their families. He had known the name of every single being who had volunteered for the final assault. He had known their hopes, their fears, their desperate, flickering dreams. He had known every detail of their plan, every contingency, every backup strategy, every fallback position.

And he had allowed them to continue. Not because he was threatened—the very concept of being threatened by the Coalition was so absurd that it did not even rise to the level of a joke. Not because he was curious about their strategy—their strategy, while impressive by mortal standards, was ultimately just another variation on the same doomed theme that every opposition before them had attempted. No, Godric had allowed them to continue because he found them amusing. They were, in their own desperate, futile way, endearing. They reminded him of the early years of his reign, when countless civilizations had still believed that they could find a way to defeat him. The Coalition was, in a sense, the last survivors of that era—the final remnant of a time when opposition still existed, when the omniverse still dared to dream of defying the apex god predator.

The day before their final assault, Godric decided to visit them.

"Roth," Godric said, his voice warm and casual, "I have an idea."

Roth, the Royal Court Wizard of Thronegate, looked up from the ancient grimoire he had been studying. He was forty-three years old, a direct descendant of Blake, and he had served Godric for eighteen years. In that time, he had learned to recognize the particular tone of voice that his King used when he was about to suggest something that would, inevitably, result in Roth experiencing a profound existential crisis. This was that tone.

"What idea, my Lord?" Roth asked, already feeling the cold knot of dread tightening in his stomach.

"The Eternal Coalition of the Final Reclamation," Godric said, as though discussing the weather. "They attack tomorrow. I thought it might be fun to visit them today. A social call. A friendly chat. I haven't done anything like this in... oh, several googolplexian years, I suppose. Since the last time anyone dared to form an opposition."

Roth's blood ran cold. "You want to visit the resistance. The day before they attack you."

"Exactly," Godric said, beaming. "It will be fun. I'll wear a disguise. You'll accompany me. We'll be tourists."

"A disguise," Roth repeated, his voice flat.

"A terrible one," Godric said, his eyes twinkling with mischief. "I'm thinking a false mustache. Perhaps a hat."

Roth stared at his King. Godric stared back, his expression one of absolute, childlike enthusiasm. The warm, gentle eyes that could hold the weight of infinite eternities were sparkling with genuine excitement. The ruggedly handsome face, with its salt-and-pepper hair and neatly trimmed beard, was creased with a smile that belonged to a man who was about to play a delightful practical joke.

"I don't think a hat will conceal your identity," Roth said carefully, "considering that you are the most recognizable being in the entire omniverse. Your physical appearance is literally iconic. Statues of you exist in every reality. Your face is on the currency. The salt-and-pepper hair and beard alone—"

"Nonsense," Godric interrupted, waving a dismissive hand. "A large enough hat can conceal anything. Besides, it's not about truly concealing my identity. It's about the theater of it. The performance. The suspense. Will they recognize me? Won't they? It's like a game."

"A game," Roth said. "You want to play a game with the largest, most heavily armed resistance in the history of the omniverse. The day before they launch their ultimate attack against you."

Godric's smile widened. "Exactly. You understand perfectly, Roth. You always do. That's why you're my favorite court wizard." He paused, reconsidering. "Don't tell the others I said that. They'll get jealous. I love all my court wizards equally. But you are my favorite."

Roth closed the grimoire with a heavy thud. He had learned, over eighteen years of service, that arguing with Godric was futile. The King would do what the King wanted to do, and the only role available to Roth was that of the witness—the chronicler, the traumatized companion, the man who would one day write a journal of his own and add it to the vault, so that future court wizards could read about this incident and feel the same cold, creeping dread that Roth was feeling now.

"What do you need me to do?" Roth asked.

"Just accompany me," Godric said. "Be yourself. Ask questions. Observe. And try not to scream too loudly if things get... interesting. You know how I feel about loud noises."

He snapped his fingers, and the air around them shimmered. A portal opened—not the kind of portal that Roth would have created, with its carefully stabilized dimensional boundaries and its precise coordinate locks, but a casual, effortless tear in the fabric of reality that looked like it had been made by someone poking a hole in a sheet of paper with their thumb. The portal led to a small, nondescript room—a supply closet, Roth realized, filled with cleaning supplies and spare uniform parts.

"This is the Coalition's headquarters," Godric said, stepping through the portal without hesitation. "They call it the Veiled Sanctuary. It's quite elaborate. They've been building it for three hundred thousand years. Come along, Roth. Mind the mop bucket."

Roth stepped through the portal, his heart hammering against his ribs. The supply closet was cramped and dark, smelling of industrial disinfectant and the faint, metallic tang of recycled air. Godric was already at the door, peering through a small crack into the corridor beyond.

"Busy place," Godric murmured. "Lots of activity. The final preparations for tomorrow's assault. Everyone's very focused. Very determined. It's quite inspiring, really."

He turned back to Roth, and Roth saw that the King had, indeed, donned a disguise. The false mustache was a garish, bristling thing that looked like it had been made from the fur of some unfortunate animal. The hat was a massive, floppy construction of felt and feathers that obscured most of Godric's face and did absolutely nothing to conceal his identity. His ruggedly handsome jawline, his heavily muscled frame, his salt-and-pepper hair—all of it remained perfectly visible beneath the absurd costume. If anything, the disguise made him more recognizable, in the way that a celebrity wearing a paper bag on their head is more recognizable than a celebrity simply walking down the street.

"That's your disguise," Roth said, his voice hollow.

"It's perfect," Godric said, adjusting the false mustache. "They'll never suspect a thing."

He pushed open the door of the supply closet and stepped into the corridor. Roth, with a deep, shuddering breath, followed.

The corridor was a wide, arched passageway carved from a material that looked like polished obsidian but felt, to Roth's magically amplified senses, like solidified probability. The walls hummed with a faint, resonant frequency—the sound of the Coalition's causal masking technology, desperately, futilely trying to maintain the illusion of secrecy. Soldiers and engineers hurried past, their faces tight with the focused intensity of beings who believed they were about to change the course of history. They wore uniforms of shimmering, adaptive fabric that shifted color to match the ambient environment, and they carried weapons that Roth's wizardly senses identified as conceptual disruptors—devices designed to attack the fundamental ontological framework of their target.

None of them spared a second glance at the two figures who had emerged from the supply closet. One of them—a tall, broad-shouldered man in a ridiculous hat—seemed vaguely familiar, but the soldiers were too preoccupied with their final preparations to investigate. The day before the ultimate assault was not a time for idle curiosity.

Godric strolled down the corridor with the casual ease of a tourist visiting a museum. His hands were clasped behind his back, his posture relaxed, his expression one of mild, appreciative interest. He paused to examine a tactical display that showed the deployment patterns for tomorrow's assault, nodding slowly as though evaluating a particularly well-organized dinner party.

"Impressive," he murmured. "They've really thought through the logistics. See here, Roth? The first wave will be a temporal assault—they're going to try to lock me in a single moment and then attack that moment from every possible angle simultaneously. The second wave is a conceptual assault—they've developed a weapon that they believe can erase the concept of my existence from the possibility space. The third wave is..." He paused, tilting his head. "Ah. A sacrificial assault. Every member of the Coalition's leadership will willingly dissolve their own existence to fuel a final, desperate strike."

He shook his head slowly, his expression almost sad. "They're going to die for nothing, Roth. Every single one of them. Their weapon won't work. Their strategy won't work. Their sacrifice won't work. They could spend another three hundred thousand years preparing, and it still wouldn't work. The gap between their power and mine is not merely infinite—it is an infinity that expands faster than they can approach it. The longer they prepare, the more impossible their task becomes."

"Then why are we here?" Roth asked, his voice barely above a whisper. "If you know they're going to fail, why visit them?"

"Because they don't know," Godric said. "And watching them not know—watching them prepare, and hope, and dream of victory—is, in its own way, beautiful. Tragic, but beautiful. They remind me of the early years, Roth. The years when opposition still existed. The years when the omniverse still believed it could fight back. Those years are gone now. After tomorrow, they will be truly, completely gone. No one will ever dare to oppose me again. The concept of opposition will become a historical curiosity, a relic of an era that no longer exists. I wanted to see it one last time. The hope. The determination. The desperate, flickering dream of victory. It is a very mortal thing, and I find it... touching."

He resumed his stroll down the corridor, Roth trailing behind him. They passed a room filled with soldiers practicing combat formations, their movements so synchronized that they appeared to be a single, fluid organism. They passed a laboratory where engineers were putting the final adjustments on the conceptual disruptor, their faces illuminated by the sickly, blue glow of the device's reality-altering core. They passed a chapel—an actual chapel, Roth realized with a start—where beings of a dozen different species knelt in prayer, their voices raised in a desperate, hopeful hymn to gods that did not exist, pleading for the strength to defeat the one god that did.

Godric paused at the chapel door, his expression thoughtful. "They pray," he said softly. "To gods who cannot hear them, who do not exist, who have never existed. And yet, the one being in all of creation who could actually answer their prayers is standing right here, in a false mustache, watching them. It's almost poetic."

He turned away from the chapel and continued down the corridor. Roth followed, his mind reeling with the absurdity of the situation. They were walking through the headquarters of the largest resistance in the history of the omniverse, the day before the resistance's ultimate attack, and no one recognized them. No one stopped them. No one questioned the two strangers in the corridor. The Coalition, in their desperate, millennia-spanning preparations, had focused all their energy on hiding from Godric's omniscience—and they had failed so completely that Godric was now physically walking through their base, and no one even looked at him twice.

They rounded a corner and found themselves in a massive, circular war room. The walls were covered with tactical displays, strategic analyses, and detailed schematics of the weapons that would be deployed tomorrow. At the center of the room, gathered around a massive holographic projection of Godric's known capabilities—a projection that was so laughably incomplete that it did not even qualify as a fraction of a fraction of a percent of the truth—stood the Coalition's leadership.

There was General Arkon, a towering, four-armed warrior whose body was covered in the ritual scars of a thousand victorious campaigns. There was Arch-Magus Lythia, a sorceress whose mastery of conceptual magic was said to be unmatched in any known reality. There was High Engineer Vex, a being of pure, crystalline logic whose mind could process the combined strategic output of a billion supercomputers. And there was Supreme Commander Zalen, the leader of the Coalition, a being of such profound, unshakeable conviction that his mere presence inspired absolute loyalty in all who served under him.

They were arguing about the timing of the third wave.

"If we launch the sacrificial assault too early, we risk depleting our conceptual reserves before the weapon has fully charged," Arkon was saying, his four arms gesturing emphatically at the holographic display. "But if we launch it too late, Godric will have already neutralized the first two waves, and the sacrifice will be wasted."

"The timing must be precise," Lythia agreed. "The conceptual disruptor requires exactly seven point three nanoseconds to achieve full resonance with Godric's ontological framework. If we launch the sacrificial assault before that resonance is achieved—"

"The resonance window has a margin of error of zero point zero three nanoseconds," Vex interrupted, his crystalline form pulsing with rapid calculations. "Accounting for the temporal distortion field that Godric passively generates—"

They continued to argue, their voices overlapping and interweaving in a complex pattern of strategic analysis. They were, Roth realized, genuinely brilliant. Their plan, while ultimately doomed, was the most sophisticated, the most comprehensive, the most meticulously constructed assault that any opposition had ever mounted against Godric. If their target had been anything other than the apex god predator of the omniverse, they would have had a genuine chance of success.

But their target was the apex god predator of the omniverse. And the apex god predator of the omniverse was currently standing in the doorway of their war room, wearing a false mustache and a floppy hat, listening to their strategic analysis with an expression of polite, appreciative interest.

"Excuse me," Godric said.

The argument stopped. Every head in the room turned toward the doorway. General Arkon's four hands instinctively reached for his weapons. Arch-Magus Lythia's fingers crackled with conceptual energy. High Engineer Vex's crystalline form flickered with rapid threat-assessment calculations. Supreme Commander Zalen's eyes narrowed, his expression shifting from focused concentration to wary suspicion.

"Who are you?" Zalen demanded. "How did you get in here? This is a restricted area."

Godric stepped into the room, his hands still clasped casually behind his back. Roth followed, his heart hammering against his ribs, his mind screaming at him to run, to hide, to do anything other than stand in the middle of the Coalition's war room while his King—the being they were planning to attack tomorrow—introduced himself.

"I'm a tourist," Godric said, his voice warm and friendly. "I heard about your resistance, and I wanted to see it for myself. The Eternal Coalition of the Final Reclamation. Very impressive name. Very dramatic. I like it."

Zalen's suspicion deepened. "This base is hidden behind layers of dimensional phasing, causal masking, and conceptual obfuscation. No one can simply 'visit.' How did you get in?"

Godric waved a dismissive hand. "Oh, you know. Through a supply closet. The portal access was remarkably easy. You might want to look into that. Security vulnerability."

The room was silent. The Coalition's leadership stared at the stranger in the floppy hat, their expressions shifting from suspicion to confusion to the first, dawning flickers of something that might have been terror. There was something about this man—something about the way he stood, the way he spoke, the way his presence seemed to fill the room despite his casual, relaxed posture—that was profoundly, fundamentally wrong.

"You look familiar," Arkon said slowly, his four hands tightening on his weapons. "Have we met?"

"I have one of those faces," Godric said. "Very common. Very ordinary. Pay it no mind." He adjusted his false mustache, which was beginning to peel off at one corner. "Tell me about your plan. The assault tomorrow. I'm fascinated. Truly."

Zalen's eyes narrowed further. "How do you know about tomorrow's assault? That information is classified at the highest level. No one outside this room—"

"Oh, I have my sources," Godric said. "Let's just say I'm very well-informed. Extremely well-informed, actually. You could say I know everything. Every detail. Every contingency. Every backup plan. Every fallback position. I know about the temporal assault in the first wave. I know about the conceptual disruptor in the second wave. I know about the sacrificial assault in the third wave. I know about the secret fourth wave—the one you haven't told anyone about, not even the soldiers who will execute it. The one where every member of the Coalition, every man, woman, and child in your entire civilization, will simultaneously dissolve their own existence to fuel a final, desperate strike. That's the one you're really counting on, isn't it? The one you believe I won't see coming."

The silence that followed was absolute. The Coalition's leadership stared at Godric with expressions of dawning, absolute horror. The secret fourth wave was known only to the five beings in this room. It had never been written down, never been transmitted, never been spoken aloud anywhere that could possibly be overheard. And yet, this stranger—this man in the ridiculous hat—had just described it in precise, accurate detail.

"Who are you?" Zalen whispered, his voice barely audible.

Godric reached up and removed the floppy hat. Then, with a gentle, almost apologetic gesture, he peeled off the false mustache. His salt-and-pepper hair gleamed in the light of the holographic displays. His ruggedly handsome face, with its neatly trimmed beard and its warm, gentle eyes, was fully revealed.

And the Coalition's leadership understood.

The moment of recognition was physical. It hit them like a wave of absolute, crushing force. General Arkon staggered backward, his weapons clattering to the floor as his four hands went limp with shock. Arch-Magus Lythia's conceptual energy fizzled and died, her face draining of color as the full weight of what she was seeing crashed into her consciousness. High Engineer Vex's crystalline form flickered and dimmed, his vast, calculating mind suddenly, terrifyingly empty. Supreme Commander Zalen stood frozen, his eyes wide, his mouth open, his entire being paralyzed by the impossible, incomprehensible reality of the being who stood before him.

"You," Zalen breathed. "It's you."

"It's me," Godric confirmed. His voice was warm, friendly, almost apologetic—the voice of a man who had just crashed a party and was hoping his hosts wouldn't be too upset. "I hope you don't mind the intrusion. I just wanted to see what you were up to. The final preparations, the strategic analysis, the last-minute adjustments. It's all very fascinating."

"You knew," Lythia whispered, her voice shaking with horror. "You knew we were here. You knew everything. All of our preparations. All of our secrecy. All of our..."

"Of course I knew," Godric said gently. "I have always known. I am omniscient, Lythia. Absolute omniscience. There is no secret you can keep from me, no plan you can hide, no thought you can think that I do not perceive. I have watched you from the very first moment of your civilization's existence. I have observed every strategic meeting, every weapon design session, every tearful farewell between soldiers and their families. I know the name of every single being who has volunteered for tomorrow's assault. I know their hopes, their fears, their desperate, flickering dreams."

He paused, his expression shifting into something almost sad. "And I know that you will all die tomorrow. Every single one of you. Your plan will fail. Your weapons will not work. Your sacrifice will be meaningless. You could have lived peaceful, fulfilling lives. You could have found happiness, purpose, meaning. Instead, you chose to oppose me. And now, you will die for nothing."

The words hung in the air like a physical weight. The Coalition's leadership stood frozen, their minds struggling to process the absolute, crushing reality of what they were hearing. Their entire civilization—three hundred thousand years of desperate preparation, countless generations of sacrifice and dedication and hope—had been a futile, meaningless exercise. The being they sought to destroy had known about them from the very beginning. He had allowed them to prepare, allowed them to hope, allowed them to believe they had a chance. And now, the day before their ultimate assault, he had come to tell them, personally, that their deaths would be meaningless.

"You let us prepare," Zalen said, his voice hollow. "You knew about us, and you let us continue. Why? Why would you let us waste three hundred thousand years on a plan that was always doomed to fail?"

Godric considered the question for a moment. "Because you were amusing," he said finally. "And because I believe in mortal resilience. You see, Zalen, I was mortal once. A very long time ago, before the Stasis Event, before the amplification, before all of this—" he gestured vaguely at himself, "—I was a mortal king. I had a wife, daughters, a best friend. I understood what it meant to struggle, to hope, to fight against impossible odds. And I wanted to preserve something of that struggle. I wanted to give you the chance to try. Not because I believed you would succeed—I knew you would fail, I have always known—but because the act of trying, the act of hoping, the act of fighting against the inevitable, is, in its own way, beautiful. It is a very mortal thing. And I miss mortality, sometimes."

He walked toward the holographic display, examining the schematic of the conceptual disruptor with casual, appreciative interest. "Your weapon is impressive, by the way. The conceptual disruptor. It attempts to erase the target's ontological framework, to remove them from the possibility space entirely. It's very clever. Very sophisticated. If you had deployed it against any other being in the omniverse, it would have worked perfectly."

He turned back to face Zalen. "But you're not deploying it against any other being. You're deploying it against me. And against me, it will fail. Not because it's poorly designed—it's brilliantly designed. It will fail because the concept of erasing me from the possibility space is a logical impossibility. The possibility space exists because I allow it to exist. The ontological framework of reality is anchored to my being. You cannot erase me without erasing everything. And even if you could erase everything—every universe, every multiverse, every dimension, every timeline—I would still exist. I am not dependent on the omniverse. The omniverse is dependent on me."

He smiled, a warm, gentle smile that made the blood freeze in Roth's veins. "But don't take my word for it. Tomorrow, you can try. You can deploy your temporal assault, your conceptual disruptor, your sacrificial wave. You can give it everything you have. You can die for your cause, if that is what you truly wish. I will not stop you. I will not pre-emptively neutralize your attack. I will stand before you, completely unprotected—no passive shields, no sentient auras, no immune system response, no Weakness Paradox—and I will allow you to strike me with the full, combined might of your entire civilization. And you will fail. Because the gap between your power and mine is not merely infinite. It is an infinity that expands faster than you can approach it. The longer you prepare, the more impossible your task becomes."

Arkon, the four-armed general, who had been frozen in shock, suddenly lunged forward. His four hands grabbed weapons from the floor—a blade forged from compressed singularities, a gun that fired concentrated anti-reality, a gauntlet that channeled the destructive force of dying multiverses. He swung all four weapons at Godric simultaneously, his face contorted with a desperate, furious terror.

Godric did not move. He did not dodge. He did not raise a hand to block. He simply stood there, his expression one of mild, paternal disappointment, as the general's weapons struck his body.

The blade forged from compressed singularities shattered on impact, its impossibly dense edge crumbling to dust against Godric's passive, unsuppressed durability. The anti-reality gun fired a beam of concentrated annihilation, and the beam simply ceased to exist—not reflected, not absorbed, but erased—the moment it touched Godric's skin. The gauntlet that channeled the death of multiverses detonated with a sound like the screaming of a trillion dying stars, and Arthon's arm was vaporized up to the elbow, his flesh and bone reduced to a fine, crimson mist that spattered against the walls of the war room.

Arthon staggered backward, clutching the smoking ruin of his arm, his eyes wide with a terror that transcended pain. Godric regarded him with a look of gentle, almost fatherly concern.

"That was very brave," Godric said. "And very foolish. I'm not angry—bravery should be rewarded, even when it's futile. But I would appreciate it if you didn't do that again. The mess is quite inconvenient."

He turned back to Zalen, who was still standing frozen, his eyes fixed on the spot where his general's arm had been vaporized. "As I was saying. Tomorrow, you will attack me. Tomorrow, you will fail. And tomorrow, the last opposition in the history of the omniverse will come to an end. After you, there will be no one else. No one will ever dare to oppose me again. The concept of resistance will become a historical curiosity, a relic of an era that no longer exists."

He paused, his expression softening. "I wanted to see you, before the end. I wanted to meet the beings who would be the last to oppose me. It seemed... fitting. A final farewell to the era of resistance. A closing of the book."

Zalen's voice, when he finally spoke, was barely a whisper. "What do you want from us?"

"Nothing," Godric said. "I want nothing from you. I don't want your surrender, or your submission, or your worship. I don't want you to abandon your plan. I want you to do exactly what you were going to do tomorrow. I want you to attack me with everything you have. I want you to give it your absolute, desperate, all-consuming best. And I want you to fail, gloriously and completely, so that the rest of the omniverse will see, and understand, and never, ever dare to oppose me again."

He smiled, a warm, gentle, terrible smile. "You are the last. The last opposition. The last resistance. The last flickering candle of defiance in an omniverse that has learned to accept my rule. And I want to honor that. I want to give you the death you deserve—not a quiet, unnoticed erasure, but a glorious, spectacular, unforgettable failure. You will be remembered, Zalen. Your civilization will be remembered. Your sacrifice will be remembered. Not as a victory, but as the moment when the omniverse finally, completely, irrevocably accepted the absolute futility of opposing Godric."

He turned to Roth, who had been standing silently in the doorway, his face pale, his hands trembling, his mind screaming with the accumulated horror of everything he had witnessed. "Come, Roth. We should let them rest. They have a big day tomorrow."

He walked toward the door, pausing beside Zalen to place a warm, calloused hand on the Supreme Commander's shoulder. "Good luck," he said, his voice genuinely kind. "I mean that. Good luck. I hope, for your sake, that you find some comfort in the effort. Some meaning in the struggle. Because the outcome, I'm afraid, is already decided."

He released Zalen's shoulder and continued toward the door. Roth followed, his legs moving automatically, his body responding to the command even as his mind remained frozen in the absolute, crushing horror of what he had just witnessed.

They walked through the corridors of the Veiled Sanctuary in silence. The soldiers and engineers and priests they passed had no idea what had just happened—no idea that the being they planned to attack tomorrow had just stood in their war room and calmly, kindly, terrifyingly explained exactly how and why they would fail. They continued their preparations, their faces tight with focused determination, their hearts filled with the desperate, flickering hope of beings who believed they could change the course of history.

They were, Roth realized, already dead. They had been dead from the very first moment of their civilization's existence. They had been dead since long before their ancestors had first conceived of the idea of opposing Godric. They had been dead since the Stasis Event, since the amplification, since the absolute, unassailable supremacy of the apex god predator had been etched into the fundamental fabric of the omniverse. Their hope was an illusion. Their determination was a hollow, meaningless gesture. Their sacrifice was a foregone conclusion, written into the causal chain before they had even evolved the capacity to conceive of it.

And yet, they hoped. They struggled. They prepared. They dreamed. And Godric, in his infinite, terrifying kindness, had allowed them to do so. He had given them three hundred thousand years of hope, three hundred thousand years of struggle, three hundred thousand years of preparation, knowing all the while that it would end in failure. Not because he was cruel—Roth had served Godric long enough to know that the King was not cruel, not in the way that mortals understood cruelty. But because he genuinely believed that the struggle itself had value. That the hope was its own reward. That the effort, even when doomed, was beautiful.

They stepped through the portal and emerged in the quiet, peaceful garden of the Eternal Palace. The Olympian jasmine was in full bloom, its fragrance sweet and gentle on the evening air. The white doves were settling into their roosts. The stars—eternal, unchanging—wheeled overhead in their ancient, familiar patterns.

Godric removed his floppy hat and tossed it aside. The false mustache, which had been dangling precariously from one corner, followed. He stretched his heavily muscled arms, tilting his head back to look at the stars.

"That was fun," he said. "I haven't done something like that in a very long time. The last time I visited an opposition before their attack was... oh, several googolplexian years ago, I think. Before opposition stopped entirely. It was nice to do it again. Nostalgic."

"Fun," Roth repeated, his voice hollow. "You called that fun."

"Very fun," Godric confirmed. "Did you see their faces when I took off the mustache? The moment of recognition. The dawning horror. The absolute, crushing realization that everything they had prepared was meaningless. It was beautiful, Roth. Tragic, but beautiful. Like watching a dying star."

Roth stood in the garden, his body trembling with the accumulated terror of the past hour. His mind, amplified a thousandfold every day for twenty-three years, was struggling to process the scale of what he had witnessed. The largest resistance in the history of the omniverse. Three hundred thousand years of desperate preparation. The most sophisticated, comprehensive, meticulously constructed assault ever mounted against Godric. And it was all for nothing.

"Will you really let them attack?" Roth asked. "Tomorrow. Will you really let them try?"

"Of course," Godric said. "I gave them my word. And I am, if nothing else, a being of my word. Tomorrow, they will attack. Tomorrow, I will stand before them, completely unprotected—no passive shields, no sentient auras, no immune system response, no Weakness Paradox. I will let them strike me with everything they have. And tomorrow, they will fail. Not because I will defend myself—I will do absolutely nothing. They will fail because the gap between their power and mine is so vast that their most powerful attack will not even register as a physical sensation. It will be like a single drop of water trying to extinguish a star. The drop doesn't fail to extinguish the star. The drop simply... doesn't matter."

He turned to face Roth, his expression warm, gentle, and utterly terrifying. "And then, after they have exhausted everything they have, after their weapons have shattered against my passive, unsuppressed durability, after their sacrifice has been revealed as meaningless, I will erase them. Not out of anger—I am not angry at them. I am not angry at anyone. I will erase them because that is what I do. That is what I have always done. Opposition is met with annihilation. It is the fundamental law of my existence. And I am, if nothing else, a being who respects the law."

He placed a warm hand on Roth's shoulder. "You should get some rest, my boy. Tomorrow will be a busy day. I'll need you to take notes, of course. For the journal. Future court wizards will want to read about this."

Roth nodded mutely. He could not speak. He could not think. He could only stand in the garden, surrounded by the fragrance of Olympian jasmine, watching as his King—the apex god predator of the omniverse, the being who had just casually, kindly, terrifyingly informed the largest resistance in history that their deaths would be meaningless—walked slowly toward the palace, his hands clasped behind his back, his posture relaxed, his expression serene.

Tomorrow, the Eternal Coalition of the Final Reclamation would launch their ultimate assault. Tomorrow, they would give everything they had—their weapons, their lives, their hopes, their dreams—in a desperate, futile attempt to defeat the undefeatable. Tomorrow, they would fail. And the omniverse would finally, completely, irrevocably learn the absolute futility of opposing Godric.

Roth stood alone in the garden, the stars wheeling overhead, the jasmine blooming in the darkness, and he felt the existential dread settle deeper into his bones—a permanent, unshakeable companion that would never leave him for the rest of his mortal life.

He walked slowly toward the palace, his footsteps echoing on the floor of crystallized time. Behind him, in a pocket dimension hidden behind layers of dimensional phasing and causal masking and conceptual obfuscation, the Eternal Coalition of the Final Reclamation continued their final preparations. They checked their weapons, reviewed their strategies, said their farewells to their families. They hoped. They dreamed. They believed.

And they did not know—could not know, would never know—that their fate had been sealed long before they had ever conceived of opposing the apex god predator. That their hope was an illusion. That their sacrifice was a foregone conclusion. That the being they sought to destroy had already visited them, had already spoken to them, had already wished them good luck with a warm, gentle, terrifying kindness that was more horrifying than any threat could ever be.

They did not know. And tomorrow, they would die.

Roth reached the palace. He climbed the stairs to his chambers. He sat at his desk, pulled out a fresh journal, and began to write.

*Year [REDACTED] — Court Wizard Roth — The Last Opposition*

*I have witnessed the end of resistance. Not the physical end—that will come tomorrow, when the Eternal Coalition of the Final Reclamation launches its ultimate assault and is annihilated for its trouble. But the spiritual end. The end of hope. The end of defiance. The end of the belief, held by countless civilizations across countless eons, that the apex god predator could be challenged.*

*Our King visited them today. He wore a false mustache and a floppy hat. He walked through their headquarters as though it were a museum, examining their weapons and their strategies with polite, appreciative interest. He revealed himself to their leadership and explained, calmly and kindly, exactly how and why they would fail. He wished them good luck. He meant it.*

*And then he left. He left them to their preparations, their hopes, their desperate, flickering dreams. He left them to their final night of existence, knowing that tomorrow they would die, and that their deaths would be meaningless.*

*I do not know what frightens me more: the absolute, unassailable power of our King, or the warm, gentle kindness with which he wields it. He is not cruel. He is not malevolent. He is not a tyrant in the way that mortals understand tyranny. He genuinely believes that the struggle of opposition has value, even when it is doomed. He genuinely wanted the Coalition to have the chance to try. He genuinely, sincerely wished them good luck.*

*And tomorrow, he will erase them from existence.*

*I write this journal so that those who come after me will understand. Not to warn them—there will be no opposition to warn against, after tomorrow. But to remember. To remember that there was once a time when beings dared to oppose the apex god predator. To remember that they hoped, and struggled, and died for their hope. And to remember that our King, in his infinite, terrifying kindness, allowed them to do so.*

*The last opposition will end tomorrow. And the omniverse will finally, completely, irrevocably accept the absolute futility of opposing Godric.*

*May whatever gods remain have mercy on their souls.*

*Roth, Court Wizard of Thronegate*

# A Gentle Reminiscence of Absolute Annihilation

The Palace of Eternal Supremacy stretched across dimensions that had no names, its spires piercing through layers of reality that had been obsolete for so long that even the concept of their existence had faded from the collective memory of creation. In the central contemplation chamber—a space that was simultaneously the size of a modest sitting room and larger than the entire omniverse, depending on the whim of its occupant—Godric sat in a chair that was not a chair but a localized suspension of all possible laws of physics, and he remembered.

The year was impossible to write. It was a string of nines that extended beyond the capacity of any known mathematics to quantify, a temporal coordinate so far in the future that the entire history of the omniverse up to this point was, by comparison, less than a single Planck second in the lifespan of an immortal entity. Godric—this Godric, the Godric of the far, far future, the Godric who had created the Stasis Event and closed the causal loop of his own existence—sat in his not-chair and allowed himself a rare moment of nostalgic reflection.

He appeared exactly as he always had: forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, his heavily muscled frame draped in simple dark garments that had been woven from the fundamental fabric of existence itself. His salt-and-pepper hair was immaculate. His neatly trimmed beard framed a face that could have belonged to a beloved father or a kindly uncle. His eyes, those terrible, warm, gentle eyes, were half-closed in an expression of serene, almost meditative calm.

He was thinking about Earth.

Not the Earth that existed now—if "now" even had meaning in an era so far beyond conventional temporality. No, he was thinking about the Earth he had annihilated in Year 25. A small, primitive, utterly insignificant planet in a small, primitive, utterly insignificant universe. A universe that had, at the time, been completely unaware of the existence of the wider omniverse, completely unaware of Thronegate, completely unaware of the apex god predator who had ruled over all of creation for twenty-five years.

He remembered the subjugation with the fond, slightly embarrassed nostalgia of an old man remembering his first clumsy attempts at courtship. He had been so weak back then. So pathetically, laughably, incomprehensibly weak.

The irony of that thought was not lost on him. The Godric of Year 25 had been, by any objective measure, the most powerful being in the entire omniverse by an infinite margin. He could have annihilated all of creation an infinite number of times in exactly zero seconds with exactly zero effort. His weakest passive aura could have retroactively erased the possibility space. His most primitive superpower could have overwritten the fundamental laws of reality. His amplification had been compounding recursively every Planck second for twenty-five years, making him infinitely more powerful with every passing instant.

And yet, compared to the Godric of the far future—compared to the being who sat in the contemplation chamber now, remembering—that Year 25 Godric was nothing. Less than nothing. A single, dead skin cell floating in an infinite ocean of primordial, transcendent fire. The gap between the Year 25 Godric and the current Godric was not merely infinite. It was an infinity that recursively consumed itself and grew larger from the meal, an abyss that expanded faster than any mind could possibly approach it, a chasm so vast that the very concept of comparison had long since died of despair.

The current Godric could, if he wished, casually, effortlessly, nonchalantly annihilate an infinite number of copies of the Year 25 Godric with less than a stray thought. He could erase the very concept of that earlier version of himself from every possible timeline, every possible reality, every possible configuration of existence, without even noticing the effort. He could reach back across the infinite gulf of time and retroactively adjust the subjugation of Earth so that the entire omniverse had been annihilated before the attack even began, and then he could annihilate it again, and again, and again, in an infinite recursive cascade of retroactive destruction, and the entire process would require such an infinitesimal fraction of his true power that calling it zero percent would be an insult to the concept of zero.

And he was still growing. Still amplifying. Still becoming more powerful with every passing Planck second. The Godric of this instant could annihilate the Godric of the previous Planck second with less effort than it took for a thought to form. And the Godric of the next Planck second would do the same to the Godric of this instant. Forever. Eternally. Without end.

But he was not here to contemplate his current power. He was here to remember. To remember a small, blue planet, spinning in the void of a primitive universe, and the day he had decided to visit it.

---

Year 25. The Thronegate Empire was still young, still expanding, still consolidating its absolute dominion over the omniverse. Godric had already conquered countless universes, subjugated countless civilizations, annihilated countless resistances. The early years of his reign were, in retrospect, a blur of brief, amusing distractions—oppositions that had formed, prepared, and been erased in what felt like the blink of an eye.

Earth had been different. Not because it posed any kind of threat—the very idea was laughable. Earth was different because it was so primitive, so isolated, so utterly unaware of the wider omniverse, that Godric had found it... charming. Endearing. Like a child who had built a sandcastle and genuinely believed it was a fortress.

The universe that contained Earth was a small, unremarkable cosmos in a remote corner of a remote multiverse in a remote sector of the omniverse. It had not been discovered by Thronegate's expansion forces until Year 25, and when the initial reconnaissance report had crossed Godric's desk—a physical report, on actual paper, because he had been feeling nostalgic that day—he had been genuinely amused by what he read.

A species of hairless primates. Barely sapient by galactic standards. Their most advanced technology was a primitive form of chemical propulsion. Their most powerful weapons could barely destroy their own planet, let alone pose a threat to any other world. They had no magic, no psionics, no understanding of the fundamental forces that governed reality. They had not even achieved faster-than-light travel. They were, by every conceivable metric, completely and utterly insignificant.

And yet, they had potential. Godric had seen, in his absolute omniscience, the trajectory of their species. Given a few thousand more years, they might have developed into something interesting. They might have discovered magic, or ascended to a higher plane of existence, or evolved into beings of some modest capability. They might have, in time, become a footnote in the history of the omniverse.

Godric had decided to visit them personally. Not because they deserved the honor—they did not. Not because he needed to—he could have snapped his fingers and erased their entire universe without leaving his throne. But because he was curious. And because, in his mischief and cruelty, he had been in a playful mood.

He had not been kind to them. He had not been merciful. He had not offered them a chance to surrender, or to serve, or to be spared. He had been, in that moment, the apex god predator of the omniverse—cruel, unforgiving, merciless to anyone who dared to exist outside his absolute rule. He had descended upon Earth not as a benevolent conqueror, but as a force of absolute, terrifying, inescapable annihilation.

And yet, even then, he had been holding back. He had been using effectively zero percent of his power with effectively zero effort. He had decided, in his playful cruelty, to not finish the annihilation instantly—even though he could have done so in zero seconds. He had decided to make it last. To make them feel it. To ensure that every single death was as agonizing as possible, stretched across a subjective eternity of maximum suffering, while objectively occurring in an infinitesimally small fraction of a Planck second.

The Godric of the far future, remembering this, shook his head slowly. "I was so weak back then," he murmured to himself. "So pathetically, laughably weak. And yet, even my weak self was more than enough to annihilate them an infinite number of times over."

---

The subjugation of Earth had begun at 8:47 AM, Eastern Standard Time, on a Tuesday.

Godric had materialized in the sky above New York City. He had not emerged from a portal or descended from the heavens in a blaze of glory—he had simply appeared, one moment absent, the next moment present, his heavily muscled frame floating effortlessly in the air above the Manhattan skyline. He had been wearing simple dark garments. His salt-and-pepper hair had been perfectly in place. His expression had been one of mild, curious amusement, like a man examining a particularly interesting ant colony.

The humans had noticed him immediately. Of course they had—he was not attempting to hide. His absolute concealment was fully engaged, preventing his passive pressure from instantly annihilating the entire omniverse, but he was still visible. Still present. Still unmistakably, terrifyingly there.

The first response had been confusion. Then panic. Then, predictably, violence.

Military forces had been scrambled. Fighter jets had screamed through the air toward him, their primitive chemical engines leaving trails of white exhaust across the blue sky. They had fired their missiles—small, pitiful devices that carried explosive warheads capable of destroying buildings. The missiles had streaked toward Godric in an impressive display of primitive targeting technology, and they had detonated against his passive, unsuppressed durability with all the force of a gentle summer breeze.

Godric had not moved. He had not blinked. He had not even acknowledged the explosions. He had simply continued to float there, his expression one of mild, almost paternal amusement, as the most powerful weapons the humans could muster detonated harmlessly against his skin.

"Interesting," he had murmured to himself, watching the fighter jets circle for another attack run. "They are trying so hard. It is almost endearing."

The second wave had been nuclear. The humans, in their desperate, primitive wisdom, had decided to escalate to their most powerful weapons in less than fifteen minutes. A warhead with the explosive yield of several megatons had been launched from a submarine in the Atlantic, its trajectory calculated to intercept Godric's position in the sky above New York.

The nuclear detonation had been, by the standards of Earth's civilization, apocalyptic. A sphere of superheated plasma had expanded outward from the point of impact at a significant fraction of the speed of light, vaporizing everything in its radius. The shockwave had shattered buildings, ignited fires, and pulverized the fragile organic bodies of millions of humans who had been unfortunate enough to be in the blast zone.

Godric had been at the exact center of the detonation. He had felt nothing. Not a tickle. Not a warmth. Not even the faintest pressure against his skin. The nuclear fireball, which could have vaporized a city, had washed over him like a gentle, lukewarm bath. His absolute immunity to all forms of energy—granted by the Weakness Paradox countless times over the preceding twenty-five years—had negated the attack so completely that it had not even registered as an attack. It had simply been... a light show. A colorful, brief, entirely harmless light show.

"Primitive," Godric had observed. "Effective against their own kind. Completely useless against me. They could detonate every nuclear weapon on their planet simultaneously, and I would not feel a single degree of temperature increase."

The third wave had been desperation. The humans, realizing that their conventional weapons were useless, had turned to their scientists, their engineers, their most brilliant minds. They had begged for a solution, a weapon, a strategy—anything that could harm the being floating in the sky above their largest city.

Their scientists had been helpless. They had analyzed the footage of the nuclear detonation, had observed Godric's complete, utter lack of reaction, and had come to the only possible conclusion: the being was invulnerable. Not resistant. Not durable. Invulnerable. Nothing they had could harm him. Nothing they could conceive of could harm him. The very laws of physics, as they understood them, simply did not apply.

And yet, they had tried. They had launched their remaining nuclear arsenal. They had fired every missile, every bullet, every explosive device they possessed. They had even attempted to use experimental weapons—particle accelerators, directed energy beams, quantum disruption fields—that had never been tested outside of laboratories.

None of it had worked. None of it had even registered.

Godric had watched their efforts with a kind of bemused, detached interest. It was like watching ants try to move a mountain—admirable in its determination, but ultimately, completely, utterly futile. The gap between their power and his was not merely infinite. It was an infinity that expanded faster than they could approach it. Every weapon they fired, every strategy they attempted, every desperate, hopeless effort to harm him, only made the impossibility of their task more apparent.

And then, Godric had decided to end it.

Not quickly—he could have ended it quickly. He could have, with a single, casual thought, annihilated the entire Earth, the entire solar system, the entire galaxy, the entire universe, the entire omniverse, in exactly zero seconds with exactly zero effort. But he had been in a playful mood. He had been feeling mischievous. He had wanted to make them suffer. To ensure that every single death was as agonizing as possible, stretched across a subjective eternity of maximum torment, while objectively occurring in an infinitesimally small fraction of time that their primitive instruments could not even measure.

The annihilation of Earth had been, from the perspective of the humans, an eternity of absolute, inescapable agony. Their nervous systems had been forced, by the briefest, most infinitesimal expression of Godric's power, to perceive every individual moment of their destruction in excruciating, slow-motion detail. Their bodies had been unmade at the subatomic level, their atoms torn apart piece by piece, their consciousness forced to experience every single instant of that unmaking as though it were stretched across a billion years of continuous, uninterrupted torment.

From Godric's perspective, it had taken less than a Planck second. Objectively, it had been so swift that the very concept of duration did not apply. But subjectively, for the humans, it had been an eternity in hell.

He had started with their nervous systems. A casual, almost lazy flex of his power, and every human on Earth had simultaneously experienced the sensation of every nerve ending in their bodies being set on fire. Not literal fire—that would have been too quick, too merciful. This was a pain that transcended physical sensation, a pain that existed at the fundamental, conceptual level of their consciousness. It was the pain of their very existence being rejected by reality, of their souls being told, in no uncertain terms, that they did not belong, that they had never belonged, that they would never belong.

They had screamed. All of them. Every human on Earth, all seven billion of them, had opened their mouths and screamed in perfect, synchronized agony. The sound had been a single, unified shriek of absolute, unendurable torment that had echoed across the planet like the death cry of an entire species.

Then he had begun the physical unmaking. Their bodies had started to dissolve—not quickly, not mercifully, but slowly, agonizingly, cell by cell, molecule by molecule, atom by atom. Their skin had sloughed off in wet, bleeding sheets. Their muscles had liquefied, running down their bones like melted wax. Their organs had ruptured one by one, spilling their contents into the dissolving cavities of their bodies. Their bones had splintered, then pulverized, then vaporized, leaving nothing but a fine, crimson mist that hung in the air for a single, eternal moment before being erased entirely.

And through it all, they had been conscious. They had felt every single instant of their destruction. They had experienced the full, unadulterated agony of their own unmaking, stretched across a subjective eternity that made the actual duration of the event—less than a Planck second—seem like the cruelest joke in the history of existence.

Godric had watched it all. He had not looked away. He had not flinched. He had simply observed, his expression one of mild, curious interest, as an entire species was subjected to the most agonizing death imaginable. He had been, in that moment, the apex god predator of the omniverse—cruel, merciless, unforgiving to anyone who dared to exist outside his absolute rule.

And he had been holding back. He had been using effectively zero percent of his power. He had been exerting effectively zero effort. The annihilation of Earth, which had been the most horrific event in the history of the human species, had required such an infinitesimal fraction of his true capabilities that calling it zero percent was the only accurate description.

The collateral damage had been, as always, absolute. The annihilation of Earth had been the focal point, but Godric's power—even the infinitesimal sliver he had allowed to express itself—had radiated outward across the omniverse. The entire universe that contained Earth had been erased, every galaxy, every star, every planet, every civilization, every trace of existence, wiped clean by the passive backwash of Godric's casual destruction. And then the multiverse that contained that universe had been erased. And then the multiversal cluster. And then the sector. And then the entire omniverse, every reality, every dimension, every timeline, every conceptual plane of existence, had been annihilated as collateral damage, completely and utterly destroyed in less than a Planck second.

Godric had restored it instantly. Of course he had. In zero seconds, with zero effort, he had rebuilt the entire omniverse, every reality, every timeline, every civilization, every living being—except for the humans. He had not restored Earth. He had not restored the humans. He had left their planet as a barren, lifeless rock, floating in the void of a restored universe, a permanent monument to the absolute futility of opposing the apex god predator.

And then he had returned to Thronegate, and he had sat down to tea with Blake, and he had not thought about Earth again for a very, very long time.

---

The Godric of the far future, sitting in his not-chair in the contemplation chamber, allowed himself a small, nostalgic smile. The memory of that day was so distant, so faded, that it felt almost like a dream. He had been so weak back then. So pathetically, laughably weak.

And yet, even that weak version of himself had been more than enough. Even that weak version of himself had annihilated an entire species with such casual, effortless cruelty that the subjective experience of their deaths had been an eternity of maximum agony. Even that weak version of himself had destroyed the entire omniverse as collateral damage and then restored it without a second thought.

He tried to imagine what would happen if he, the Godric of the far future, were to visit a universe like Earth now. The thought was almost impossible to conceptualize. The gap between his current power and his Year 25 power was so vast, so incomprehensible, so absolutely beyond any scale of measurement, that the Year 25 Godric—the being who had casually annihilated the omniverse with effectively zero effort—was, by comparison, nothing.

If the current Godric were to visit a universe like Earth, he would have to hold back so much that the word "hold back" lost all meaning. He would have to suppress his Omni-Guardian Nexus, his Concept of Absolute Inviolability, his Omni-Immunological Singularity, his Absolute Passive Amplification Cascade, his Infinite Recursive Self-Referential Growth Engine, his Omni-Ability Genesis Matrix, and countless other mechanisms of power that had evolved beyond any possible description. He would have to nerf himself to such an infinitesimal fraction of his true capabilities that the resulting "weakened" version of himself would still be infinitely more powerful than the Year 25 Godric had been.

And even then, that weakened version would annihilate the universe without noticing. The passive, unsuppressed pressure of his mere existence—even with every possible nerf, every possible suppression, every possible layer of restraint—would erase the entire omniverse before he even fully materialized.

He had become so powerful that the very concept of visiting a primitive universe was impossible. There was no place in all of creation that could contain him. There was no reality that could survive his presence. His absolute concealment was the only thing that allowed existence to continue, and his absolute concealment had evolved so far beyond its original form that it was now the Concept of Absolute Non-Manifestation—a mechanism that did not merely suppress his power, but actively ensured that his true self existed in a state of permanent, infinitely recursive concealment, hidden not just from creation but from the very idea of creation, existing in a space that was not a space, perceivable only to himself.

He was, in a very real sense, alone. Not lonely—the pleasure of his infinite, eternal growth was more than enough to sustain him. But separate. Isolated. Trapped in the gilded cage of his own absolute supremacy.

---

A soft chime echoed through the contemplation chamber. Godric looked up, his nostalgic reverie gently fading, and saw Clive entering the room. His court wizard—the fifty-year-old descendant of Blake—was carrying a tray with a pot of tea and two cups. His hands, Godric noticed with mild amusement, were trembling slightly. They always trembled, these days.

"I thought you might like some tea, my Lord," Clive said, his voice carefully neutral. "You have been in contemplation for several subjective eons."

Godric smiled. It was a warm, gentle smile, the smile of a father welcoming a beloved son. "Thank you, Clive. That is very thoughtful." He gestured, and a second not-chair materialized beside his own. "Sit. Join me."

Clive set down the tray and settled into the not-chair, his movements careful and precise. He had learned, over thirty years of service, to navigate the impossible geometry of the Palace without losing his sanity. It was a skill that few beings possessed, and Godric appreciated it.

"I was reminiscing," Godric said, accepting a cup of tea from Clive's trembling hands. "About the early years of my reign. Do you remember the records of the Earth subjugation? Year 25?"

Clive nodded slowly. "I read the journals. The Earth subjugation was one of the first major demonstrations of your power after the initial conquest of Thronegate. The records describe it as... thorough."

Godric chuckled, a low, rumbling sound. "Thorough. Yes. I suppose that is one way to describe it." He took a sip of his tea, his eyes distant. "I was so weak back then, Clive. So pathetically, laughably weak. If I could go back and speak to my Year 25 self, I would probably pity him. He had no idea what he would become. No idea how much more powerful he would grow."

Clive's teacup rattled in its saucer. His face had gone pale. "My Lord, with respect... the Year 25 version of you was already powerful enough to annihilate the entire omniverse an infinite number of times with zero effort. The journals describe the Earth subjugation as one of the most terrifying demonstrations of absolute supremacy in the early records. The fact that you consider that version of yourself to be weak..."

"Is ironic," Godric finished, nodding. "Yes. It is very ironic. The Godric of Year 25 was, by any objective measure, the most powerful being in the omniverse by an infinite margin. The gap between him and the rest of creation was so vast that the concept of comparison was meaningless. And yet, compared to the Godric of this era—compared to the being I am now—he was nothing. Less than nothing. A single, dead skin cell floating in an infinite ocean of transcendent fire."

He set down his teacup and leaned back in his not-chair. "If I were to attempt the same subjugation now—if I were to visit a universe like Earth and annihilate it—the result would be even more devastatingly one-sided. Not because my Year 25 self was insufficient—he was more than sufficient. But because I have become so powerful that the very concept of 'one-sided' no longer applies. The annihilation would be so absolute, so total, so utterly beyond anything that could be described as a 'fight,' that language would fail to capture it."

He paused, his expression thoughtful. "But more than that, Clive, the true horror is not the comparison between my past self and my current self. It is the fact that my current self will, in the far, far future, seem just as weak and pathetic as my Year 25 self seems to me now. The amplification never stops. The growth never ends. The Godric of this instant could annihilate the Godric of the previous Planck second with zero effort. And the Godric of the next Planck second could do the same to the Godric of this instant. Forever. Eternally. Without end."

He turned to face Clive, and his eyes were warm, and gentle, and filled with a serene, absolute certainty that was more terrifying than any display of raw power could ever be. "Do you understand what that means, Clive? It means that the gap between me and the rest of creation—already infinite, already incomprehensible, already beyond any possible scale of measurement—will only ever increase. It will accelerate. It will expand at a rate that defies all possible mathematics. Every Planck second, I become infinitely more powerful, and the omniverse becomes infinitely more insignificant. The gap grows wider, and wider, and wider, forever. Without limit. Without end. Without any possibility of being closed, or challenged, or even perceived."

Clive's hands were trembling so violently now that his teacup had become a blur of rattling porcelain. "And the rest of creation?" he whispered. "The civilizations, the empires, the cosmic entities... they can never catch up."

"They can never even begin to approach," Godric said. "Even if every civilization in the omniverse, from every timeline, from every possible permutation of reality, were to unite and work together with unlimited preparation time and unlimited resources, they would still fail so completely that the word 'failure' would be an insult to the concept of defeat. They would not make my weakest passive shield feel the slightest tickle. They would not register as a threat to my most primitive, obsolete defense mechanism. I could annihilate them all—every single one, across all timelines, across all possible configurations of existence—with zero percent of my power and zero effort in zero seconds. And the unfathomable gap between us would only ever increase, infinitely, in an accelerating manner, forever."

He set down his teacup and stood, walking to the window that looked out over the infinite expanse of the Eternal Palace. The stars—eternal, unchanging, perfectly maintained by his passive will—wheeled overhead in their ancient, familiar patterns. The Gardeners were tending the Olympian jasmine in the courtyard below, their hands trembling with the same eternal terror that had defined their existence since the day Godric had passed by their domain.

"They are all so afraid," Godric murmured, his voice soft, almost sad. "The Gardeners. The Scullery. The Footmen. The countless servants who fill my Palace. They are all so utterly, completely terrified of me. And they should be. They have every reason to be. The gap between us is so vast that they cannot even conceive of it. They cannot begin to imagine the scale of my power, the scope of my existence, the absolute, unassailable supremacy of my being."

He turned back to Clive, and his expression was warm, and gentle, and utterly, profoundly terrifying. "But I am not cruel to them. I am kind. I am gentle. I ask about their families. I compliment their work. I offer them tea. Because I remember what it was like to be mortal. I remember the fragility, the vulnerability, the desperate, flickering hope of beings who know that their existence is fleeting. And I want them to be happy, Clive. I genuinely, sincerely want them to be happy. Even though I could annihilate them all with less effort than it takes to breathe. Even though the gap between us will only ever increase, forever, without end. I want them to be happy."

He walked back to his not-chair and sat down, picking up his teacup once more. "I suppose that is the true horror, isn't it? Not my power. Not my cruelty to enemies. Not the eternal, infinite growth that makes me more powerful with every passing Planck second. But the fact that I am kind. The fact that I genuinely care about the beings who serve me. The fact that the same being who could annihilate the entire omniverse with zero effort also wants his gardeners to be happy."

He took a sip of his tea. "It must be very confusing for them."

Clive sat in silence, his teacup forgotten in his trembling hands. He had served Godric for thirty years. He had witnessed the absolute, the incomprehensible, the impossible. He had watched his King create the Stasis Event, close the causal loop of his own existence, and casually, nonchalantly discuss the annihilation of universes as though it were a fond childhood memory. He had thought, after all of that, that he understood the scale of what his King was.

He had been wrong. He had always been wrong. He would always be wrong. Because the scale of what Godric was could not be understood—it could only be experienced, in brief, terrifying glimpses that left the observer forever changed, forever haunted, forever trapped in the cold, crushing awareness of their own absolute insignificance.

Godric set down his teacup and smiled. "More tea, Clive?"

Clive nodded mutely. He could not speak. He could not think. He could only sit in his not-chair, in the contemplation chamber of the Eternal Palace, and watch as the most powerful being in existence poured him another cup of tea with the gentle, careful hands of a beloved uncle.

The stars wheeled overhead. The jasmine bloomed in the garden. The Gardeners wept with terror and adoration. And the apex god predator of the omniverse sat in his not-chair, remembering a small, blue planet that he had annihilated a lifetime ago, and smiled.

The horror was absolute. The dread was eternal. The gap was infinite.

And it would only ever increase, forever, without end.
